children.text: The algorithmic bias problem in healthcare AI has been documented primarily in urban academic medical center deployments—most notably the Optum comorbidity risk score that systematically underestimated illness severity in Black patients. The rural dimension of algorithmic bias is less studied but potentially more consequential: rural AI deployments are using tools trained almost exclusively on urban, commercially-insured populations and applying them to patient populations that differ dramatically in demographics, disease prevalence, care-seeking behavior, and social determinants profile.
The Three Bias Types Observed in Rural AI Deployments

Population Distribution Bias occurs when a model’s training data does not reflect the demographic composition of the deployment population. Rural populations are significantly older, more likely to be white or Native American (depending on region), have higher rates of certain chronic conditions, and have different healthcare utilization patterns than urban populations. A sepsis prediction model trained on urban academic medical center data will apply urban arrival-pattern assumptions to a rural patient who presents much later in the disease course—producing systematic underprediction of severity.

Geographic Proxy Bias occurs when models use ZIP code, insurance type, or proximity to specialty care as proxy variables. These variables correlate with race and socioeconomic status in ways that are well-understood in urban contexts but produce different—and sometimes inverted—effects in rural contexts. A readmission risk model that uses proximity to primary care as a negative risk factor (close to care = lower risk) will systematically underestimate risk for rural patients who live near the only available provider but have dramatically worse access to follow-up than the model predicts.

Outcome Label Bias occurs when the training outcome (e.g., 30-day readmission) is used as a proxy for disease severity but actually reflects healthcare access. A patient who is not readmitted because they lack transportation is labeled ‘low-risk’ by the training algorithm, when they may in fact have worse disease status than a high-risk patient who was readmitted. Rural populations’ utilization patterns are more strongly influenced by access barriers than by health status—making this bias type especially severe in rural model deployments.

children.text: The Governance Framework Rural Systems Must Implement

Three governance requirements are emerging as the minimum standard for responsible rural AI deployment. First, pre-deployment bias audit: a structured analysis of the training data composition versus the local patient population, with mandatory recalibration if demographic gap exceeds a defined threshold. Second, disparate impact monitoring: ongoing tracking of AI output distribution by race, ethnicity, age, and insurance type to detect post-deployment bias that was not apparent in pre-deployment testing. Third, human review requirements for high-stakes decisions: any AI output that directly affects care triage, resource allocation, or treatment selection must have a defined clinician review step with override documentation.

Deploying an AI tool without a disparate impact audit is the algorithmic equivalent of deploying a drug without clinical trials in the indication population. The absence of evidence of harm is not evidence of absence of harm.

GOVERNANCE REQUIREMENT: Before deploying any AI clinical decision support tool, rural health systems should require vendors to provide (1) training data demographic composition report, (2) performance metrics disaggregated by race and socioeconomic status, and (3) a contractual commitment to provide local recalibration support. children.text: Community health workers—frontline public health workers who are trusted members of the communities they serve—represent the most robustly evidence-supported health equity intervention for rural populations. A 2025 systematic review in the American Journal of Public Health identified 34 high-quality studies of CHW programs in rural settings, finding a median ROI of 4.8:1 (range 3.1–8.2:1) and consistent evidence of impact across chronic disease management, maternal health, mental health navigation, and social needs resolution.
Why CHWs Work in Rural Settings

The CHW’s effectiveness in rural settings derives from three factors that no clinical or technology intervention can replicate: trusted community identity (CHWs are from the communities they serve, with existing social capital and cultural competency), geographic persistence (unlike visiting clinicians, CHWs live and work in the community year-round), and care navigation capability (CHWs can navigate both the formal healthcare system and the informal community resource network simultaneously). In rural communities where distrust of formal healthcare institutions runs high, the CHW is often the only health system representative who has earned patient trust.

The CHW is not a cheaper nurse. She is a community member with clinical training. The difference matters enormously in a rural county where the hospital is seen as a place you go to die, not a resource you use to stay healthy.

children.text: The Sustainable Financing Problem—and How States Are Solving It

The most common failure mode for CHW programs is financial: they launch as grant-funded pilots, demonstrate strong outcomes, and then lose funding when the grant ends. The rural health systems and state programs that have built durable CHW infrastructure have done so by solving the financing problem through one of three mechanisms: Medicaid CHW service billing (19 states now have specific Medicaid billing codes for CHW services), FQHC scope-of-service inclusion (FQHCs that include CHWs in their scope of service receive cost-based reimbursement), or value-based contract integration (including CHW cost as a shared savings investment in AHEAD and commercial VBC contracts).

Kentucky, West Virginia, and New Mexico—three states with both significant rural health disparities and active RHT programs—have all codified Medicaid CHW billing within the past 24 months. The financial model is now proven: a CHW at a $42,000 annual salary generating Medicaid billable services at $45/encounter, with an average caseload of 80 patients and 6 encounters per patient per year, generates $21,600 in direct Medicaid revenue—covering approximately half the salary cost, with shared savings and avoided acute care costs covering the remainder.

children.text: The expansion of the CMS AHEAD (States Advancing All-Payer Health Equity Approaches and Development) Model to six additional states in 2026 marks the most significant test of global hospital budgeting in the American context since Maryland’s All-Payer system. With AHEAD now covering an estimated 12% of rural hospital spending in participating states, planners are looking to international evidence to anticipate implementation challenges that the U.S. evidence base cannot yet answer.
Canada: Global Hospital Budgets in Rural Ontario

Ontario’s Health Services Restructuring Commission introduced global operating budgets for rural and small community hospitals in the late 1990s. A 2024 retrospective by the Canadian Institute for Health Information found that rural Ontario hospitals on global budgets showed 22% lower rates of avoidable hospitalization compared to similar facilities on fee-for-service, largely driven by investment in post-acute and home care coordination that the budget flexibility enabled.

The critical implementation lesson from Ontario is the transition period. Facilities that moved to global budgets without a minimum 18-month financial bridge experienced significant operating deficits in years two and three as new care coordination infrastructure was built but old FFS revenue had already been replaced. The AHEAD program’s 36-month transition payment is calibrated precisely to avoid this cliff.
England: Integrated Care Systems as the Structural Parallel

England’s 42 Integrated Care Systems, fully operational since July 2022, are the closest structural analog to what AHEAD is attempting. ICS’ cover defined geographies, hold a combined population budget, and are accountable for both individual care and population health outcomes. A 2025 NHS England evaluation of the 14 ICS’ covering predominantly rural populations found that emergency admissions from rural areas fell 9% in the first two operational years, but GP vacancy rates—the rural workforce problem—were not materially improved by the budget model alone.
Global budgets solve the incentive problem. They do not solve the geography problem. Rural workforce requires a separate, direct intervention that no budget model alone will produce.

This shift was promised to bring efficiency and stability; instead, it brought commoditization. While often conflated, their economic structures differ significantly. DPC typically targets the mass market with a flat monthly fee (avg. $75/month) and refuses all insurance, effectively functioning as a subscription utility. Concierge medicine retains the insurance billing component but adds a substantial retainer (often $2,000+/year) for enhanced access, targeting a wealthier demographic.

In Health Economics (Bhattacharya), the demand for healthcare is treated as a derived demand for 'Health Capital.' The Grossman Model posits that individuals invest in medical care to offset the natural depreciation of their health stock. Applying this to the Vermont context, the Oliver Wyman report highlights a critical demographic variable: Vermont's aging population represents a rapidly accelerating depreciation rate of health capital. The community engagement sessions for Act 167 revealed a stark inelasticity of demand; rural populations require access regardless of price, yet the 'cost of investment' (premiums and deductibles) has outpaced the marginal utility for the commercial sector.
The Hospital Industry: Fixed Costs and Market Failure

The standard hospital firm model assumes that firms exit the market when Average Total Cost (ATC) exceeds Price. However, Vermont's hospital market is characterized by 'natural monopoly' features in rural areas. The Oliver Wyman report data indicates that many Critical Access Hospitals (CAHs) are operating where Marginal Cost is low, but high Fixed Costs (infrastructure, compliance) make solvency impossible without cross-subsidization. Act 167 attempts to address this not by market exit (closure), but by 'global budgeting'—essentially regulating the utility to ensure survival despite market failure.

children.text: CMS’s Acute Hospital Care at Home (AHCaH) waiver, first established during the COVID-19 public health emergency and extended through December 31, 2026 under the CAA, now covers 137 rural hospitals across 34 states. The Operational Model in Rural Markets

The rural Hospital-at-Home operational model differs meaningfully from urban implementations. The two-hour visit requirement, which CMS mandates for AHCaH patients, is achievable in urban markets with dense nursing staff. In rural markets with a 30–60-minute drive between patients, the same requirement demands a more geographically concentrated patient panel and a different staffing model. The rural systems achieving operational viability are limiting their HaH service area to a 20-mile radius from the hospital and deploying community paramedics—already on road for EMS—as the primary daily visit staff.

The community paramedic model is operationally elegant for rural HaH: EMS agencies are already deployed across the service area, have established patient relationships, and can provide basic clinical monitoring and medication administration within their expanded scope. The most successful rural HaH programs, including those in Rhode Island and Florida’s RHT program designs, have formalized paramedicine as the daily visit mechanism with hospital physicians providing oversight via telemedicine.

children.text: Patient Eligibility: The Rural Selection Criteria

Rural HaH programs report that 28–35% of otherwise eligible patients fail the home safety screen—primarily due to caregiver absence and substandard housing—compared to 12–18% in urban programs. This significantly affects program census projections.
The rural Hospital-at-Home program that works is not the one with the best technology. It is the one that solved the home safety problem. You cannot deliver hospital care in a home that is not safe.

By July 1, 2026, every participating hospital ED must demonstrate three core capabilities: (1) a stocked obstetric emergency cart compliant with the ACOG Hemorrhage Bundle specifications, including uterotonic medications, compression sutures, and Level I resuscitation equipment for neonates; (2) at least one registered nurse per shift with current ALSO (Advanced Life Support in Obstetrics) or NRP (Neonatal Resuscitation Program) certification; and (3) a documented transfer agreement with a facility providing comprehensive obstetric care within 60 minutes transport time.

The United States loses more women to obstetric hemorrhage in rural emergency departments than in labor and delivery units. This mandate addresses the silent front door of the maternal mortality crisis.

children.text: Editor's note (2026): This brief has been revised for accuracy. An earlier version stated that Medicaid Disproportionate Share Hospital (DSH) reductions were “legally in effect beginning FY2026.” That is not correct: although the Affordable Care Act scheduled DSH allotment cuts of roughly $8 billion per year for FY2026–FY2028, Congress has repeatedly delayed them, and the FY2026 reductions have not taken effect on the schedule the original draft assumed. The figures below are drawn from public sources (Congressional Research Service, CBO, and the Chartis Center for Rural Health).
The DSH Cliff: Scheduled, Severe — and Repeatedly Postponed

When the Affordable Care Act expanded Medicaid in 2010, its architects assumed that broader coverage would shrink uncompensated care and justify reducing Medicaid DSH payments, which compensate hospitals that serve a disproportionate share of low-income and uninsured patients. The law therefore wrote in a schedule of DSH allotment reductions — currently set at roughly $8 billion per year for FY2026, FY2027, and FY2028. The bet was only half right. In states that expanded Medicaid, uncompensated care did fall. In the ten states that did not expand, rural hospitals kept absorbing the uninsured volume the DSH mechanism was designed to offset.

Crucially, the scheduled cuts have not actually landed. Congress has postponed the DSH reductions repeatedly through short-term legislation, most recently through the appropriations process, and a one-year delay is inexpensive enough that the Congressional Budget Office has scored such a delay at roughly $625 million. The result is a recurring “cliff”: the cuts are always one funding deadline away from taking effect, which makes multi-year financial planning for the most exposed rural hospitals extraordinarily difficult even though the reductions themselves keep being deferred.
Why Rural Hospitals Are the Most Exposed

The exposure is not evenly distributed. According to the Chartis Center for Rural Health’s 2025 analysis, 46% of rural hospitals were operating with a negative margin and 432 were vulnerable to closure. The expansion gap is stark: the ten non-expansion states hold about 30% of all rural hospitals, but 53% of rural hospitals in those states were in the red, with a median operating margin of −1.5% — versus 43% in the red and a +1.5% median in expansion states. For hospitals already below break-even, a DSH cut is not a budget variance to be managed through efficiency; it removes a structural pillar of solvency.

The distribution mechanism compounds the problem. Congress sets a national DSH allotment; CMS distributes it to states by formula; and states then pay qualifying hospitals using their own methodologies — often weighted toward Medicaid inpatient days. That design systematically underweights Critical Access Hospitals, whose care is concentrated in emergency and outpatient settings rather than inpatient admissions. A reduction calibrated to high-volume urban safety-net economics is applied, largely unmodified, to low-volume rural facilities.
The Services Disappear Before the Buildings Do

Even where hospitals avoid closure, financial pressure shows up first as service-line loss. Between 2011 and 2023, 293 rural hospitals stopped offering obstetric services — nearly a quarter of all rural OB units. From 2014 to 2023, 424 rural hospitals ended chemotherapy services, about 21% of those that had offered it. These reductions widen the very access gaps — in maternal care and cancer care — where rural outcomes already lag urban ones, and they are difficult to reverse once the specialized staff have left the community.
What Hospital Leaders Should Actually Do

Because the DSH schedule keeps being deferred but never repealed, the prudent posture for an exposed rural hospital is to plan for the cut while it is still suspended. Three steps are concrete and within management’s control. First, quantify facility-specific exposure: model what a full DSH reduction would do to your margin using your own most recent DSH receipts as the baseline, rather than relying on statewide aggregates that mask facility-level distribution differences.

Second, pursue fixed-cost reduction that does not jeopardize Critical Access Hospital certification. CAH Conditions of Participation require 24/7 emergency capability and inpatient capacity but do not mandate specific specialty lines, which leaves room to consolidate or share laboratory, radiology, and revenue-cycle functions — typically the largest controllable overhead categories — through regional shared-services agreements rather than full mergers.

Third, engage early on affiliation. The window to negotiate a management-services agreement or partial affiliation from a position of relative strength closes as cash reserves shrink; distressed transactions are harder to structure and provoke more community resistance. Boards in the most exposed markets should also brief their congressional delegations with quantified, facility-specific closure risk — the kind of district-level detail that has historically driven the bipartisan votes to delay the cuts in the first place.
The Bottom Line

The DSH reductions are real, large, and still on the books — but they are not, as of this writing, in force, because Congress keeps postponing them. The danger for rural hospitals is twofold: that one of these deferrals eventually fails, and that the perpetual uncertainty itself deters the long-horizon investment rural systems need. The hospitals most likely to survive the eventual cut are those that treat the current reprieve as planning time, not relief.

children.text: Program Status

The Acute Hospital Care at Home (AHCAH) waiver, initially granted as a COVID-19 emergency measure, was extended through December 2026 by the Further Consolidated Appropriations Act. As of January 2026, 330 hospitals in 38 states are approved to provide acute-level care in patients' homes, covering conditions including pneumonia, cellulitis, COPD exacerbation, and heart failure.
Clinical Outcomes

The largest published outcomes study, covering 11,246 patients across 12 health systems (2022-2024), shows 30-day readmission rates of 6.8% for hospital-at-home versus 9.4% for matched inpatient controls — a 27.7% reduction. Mortality rates were statistically equivalent. Patient satisfaction scores were 18% higher for hospital-at-home admissions.
Cost Analysis

Average total episode cost for hospital-at-home is 30-35% below equivalent inpatient stays, driven primarily by reduced overhead allocation, elimination of facility-acquired infection costs, and reduced length-of-stay variation. For a 400-bed system diverting 5% of eligible admissions to home, estimated annual savings range from $8M to $14M.
Operational Barriers

Scaling hospital-at-home requires significant upfront investment: mobile monitoring equipment ($1,200-$2,400 per patient), clinical logistics infrastructure, and 24/7 rapid-response nursing capacity. The staffing model — requiring in-person visits twice daily plus remote monitoring — is economically viable only at volumes exceeding 150 concurrent patients for most systems.

children.text: Pharmacogenomics Coverage Landscape

Pharmacogenomic (PGx) testing enables clinicians to select medications and doses based on a patient's genetic profile, reducing adverse drug reactions and improving therapeutic efficacy. Commercial payer coverage has expanded significantly: 78% of large commercial plans cover PGx testing for at least one drug-gene pair, up from 41% in 2021.
Most Commonly Covered Tests

Drug-gene pairs with the strongest commercial coverage include: CYP2C19 for clopidogrel dosing (cardiovascular), CYP2D6 for codeine and tamoxifen (oncology and pain management), TPMT/NUDT15 for thiopurine dosing (oncology), and HLA-B*57:01 for abacavir hypersensitivity (HIV). Multi-gene panel testing — covering 25+ genes simultaneously — is covered by fewer than 40% of commercial plans.
CMS Coverage Status

Medicare coverage remains fragmented. CMS issued a Local Coverage Determination (LCD) framework in 2023 establishing coverage for PGx testing in specific oncology contexts but declined to issue a National Coverage Determination for broader PGx panels. This has created geographic variation in Medicare coverage depending on which MAC jurisdiction covers the beneficiary.

children.text: Telehealth Volume Stabilization

Following the pandemic-driven surge to 32% of outpatient visits in 2020, telehealth volumes have stabilized at approximately 12% of all outpatient encounters in 2025. This level represents an 8x increase over pre-COVID baseline of 1.4%. The stabilization suggests telehealth has achieved lasting integration into clinical workflow rather than reverting to minimal use.
Specialty Variation

Telehealth integration varies dramatically by specialty. Behavioral health leads at 38% of visits conducted virtually. Dermatology (28%), neurology (22%), and endocrinology (19%) follow. Primary care averages 14%. Surgical specialties, procedural gastroenterology, and ophthalmology remain below 5%, where hands-on examination is clinically essential.
Quality Evidence

For behavioral health — the dominant telehealth use case — outcomes data is consistently positive. PHQ-9 depression score improvement rates in telepsychiatry match or exceed in-person benchmarks in four of five published studies. HEDIS performance measures for depression follow-up at 30 and 84 days improved in health plans with high telehealth penetration.

children.text: SEP-1 Compliance Status

CMS's Severe Sepsis and Septic Shock Early Management Bundle (SEP-1) measures compliance with six specific interventions within prescribed time windows. National compliance reached 76% in 2025, up from 49% when the measure was introduced in 2015. Compliance variation by hospital type remains significant: academic medical centers average 84%, while critical access hospitals average 61%.
Mortality Correlation Controversy

The most significant challenge to SEP-1's validity is the weak correlation between bundle compliance and mortality outcomes. Analysis of 5-year Medicare data shows that hospitals with the highest SEP-1 compliance scores have sepsis mortality rates statistically indistinguishable from low-compliance hospitals. This has fueled debate about whether the bundle measures process improvements that matter clinically.
Proposed Bundle Updates

The Surviving Sepsis Campaign's 2025 guideline revision proposes replacing the time-anchored SEP-1 bundle with a treat-to-target approach emphasizing lactate-guided resuscitation endpoints. CMS has initiated a public comment period on potential SEP-1 revisions, with implementation of any updated measure not expected before 2028.

children.text: National Maternal Mortality Status

The United States recorded a maternal mortality rate of 17.9 per 100,000 live births in 2024 (CDC NCHS final data) — the highest among comparably resourced nations. That is roughly double Canada's rate (about 8 per 100,000) and several times the rates of Australia and the United Kingdom (roughly 3–6 per 100,000). After years of deterioration that peaked during the pandemic, the rate has eased modestly but remains far above its high-income peers.
State-Level Variation

Maternal mortality variation across states is dramatic and not fully explained by case mix or demographics. California (7.3 per 100,000) leads the nation following 15 years of implementing the California Maternal Quality Care Collaborative's evidence-based toolkits. Mississippi (43.1 per 100,000), Louisiana (38.4), and Oklahoma (35.7) have the worst outcomes, driven by limited access to obstetric care and high rates of chronic conditions.
Racial Disparities

Black women die from pregnancy-related causes at 3.4 times the rate of white women — a disparity that persists after controlling for income, education, and clinical risk factors. Research increasingly implicates structural racism in healthcare settings, including differential pain assessment and treatment, discharge against patient concerns, and less frequent access to high-volume obstetric centers.
Evidence-Based Interventions

The Alliance for Innovation on Maternal Health (AIM) bundles — standardized protocols for obstetric emergencies including hemorrhage, hypertension, and venous thromboembolism — have demonstrated 22-38% reduction in severe maternal morbidity in implementing hospitals. As of 2025, 41 states have adopted AIM bundles at the hospital level, though implementation fidelity varies widely.

The Medicare Shared Savings Program (MSSP) reported $2.1B in net savings to the Medicare Trust Fund in 2025, the highest since program inception in 2012. Total ACO participation grew to 512 organizations covering 11.4M beneficiaries. The distribution of savings is highly skewed toward Enhanced Track participants.
Track-Level Performance

Enhanced Track ACOs generated average per-beneficiary savings of $847, versus $212 for Basic Track Level E and minimal savings for lower Basic Track levels. The performance gap reflects Enhanced Track's two-sided risk structure, which incentivizes aggressive care management investment.
Organizational Structure Findings

Physician-led ACOs without hospital ownership outperformed hospital-led ACOs in per-beneficiary savings by 23%. This confirms prior research suggesting that hospital-led structures face incentive misalignment — hospitals benefit from inpatient volume that ACO contracts reward reducing.
Geographic Variation

Rural ACOs underperformed urban counterparts by 31% on average savings rates, despite lower baseline costs. Access limitations — particularly specialist availability and transportation — constrain care coordination effectiveness in rural settings. CMS is piloting enhanced rural flex payments in 2026.

Healthcare private equity experienced a significant recalibration in 2024-2025 following the interest rate surge of 2022-2023. With the 10-year Treasury stabilizing around 4.2%, leveraged buyout economics have normalized, but the frothy exit environment of 2019-2021 has not returned.
Sector-Specific Dynamics

Behavioral health remains the most sought-after sub-sector, with 247 transactions in 2025 (down from 312 in 2023 but stable from 2024). Dental services organizations (DSOs) faced the sharpest multiple compression, falling from 14x to 8x EBITDA as Medicaid adult dental expansions have not materialized as projected.
Regulatory Headwinds

FTC and state attorney general scrutiny of healthcare consolidation has extended deal timelines by an average of 8 months. Three PE-backed transactions were blocked outright in 2025: two anesthesiology roll-ups and one home health acquisition. FTC's 2024 policy statement on physician practice acquisitions explicitly targets roll-up strategies.

children.text: Rate Normalization

Travel registered nurse compensation peaked at an average $3,800/week in early 2022 during COVID-driven staffing crises. By Q3 2025, travel RN rates had normalized to $1,820/week — a 52% decline. Hospitals have dramatically reduced reliance on contract labor, with contract RN share of total hours falling from 12% (2022) to 4% (2025).
Structural Shortage Persists

Despite rate normalization, the Bureau of Labor Statistics projects 195,000 RN job openings annually through 2031. The American Association of Colleges of Nursing reports that U.S. nursing schools turned away 91,938 qualified applicants in 2024 due to faculty shortages, inadequate clinical placement capacity, and facility constraints.
Economic Modeling

HTR’s own modeling projects a net shortage on the order of 450,000 RNs by 2030 under the current trajectory; this is an HTR estimate, not a published government figure. The economic cost of unfilled nursing positions — accounting for vacancy costs, overtime premiums, and quality-of-care impacts — is, on HTR’s assumptions, roughly $86,000 per unfilled FTE annually, implying a burden in the tens of billions of dollars per year on U.S. hospitals.
Solutions Landscape

Three interventions show economic promise: nursing school faculty salary subsidies (ROI of 4.2:1 over 10 years), international nurse recruitment with pathway-to-permanent-residency programs (median 14-month ROI), and team-based care redesign reducing RN task burden by 22% through medical assistant and LPN task redistribution.

CMS initiated a risk adjustment model recalibration in 2024, updating the V28 HCC model to reflect more accurate diagnosis coding patterns. The updated model reduced average risk scores by approximately 3.4%, translating to reduced per-member-per-month payments for MA plans.
Financial Impact

The American Health Insurance Plans (AHIP) estimates cumulative payment reductions of $31B over 2024-2026 across the MA market. Large national plans (UnitedHealth, Humana, CVS/Aetna) have absorbed losses through scale efficiencies and supplemental benefit reductions. Regional plans face existential pressure.
Market Exit and Access

Forty-three counties — predominantly rural — lost MA plan options for 2026, forcing beneficiaries back to traditional Medicare with limited supplemental coverage options. This represents the highest rural MA exit rate since 2014 and signals potential for further access deterioration.

children.text: Compliance Landscape

Three years after CMS began substantive enforcement of hospital price transparency requirements, compliance has reached 82% for large urban hospitals but lags significantly among critical access hospitals (44%) and for-profit multi-site systems (61%). The penalty maximum of $2M per hospital per year has driven compliance among high-revenue institutions.
Data Quality Problems

Machine-readable file compliance does not equate to usable transparency. An HTR audit of 500 hospital price files found that 67% used non-standard formats incompatible with common price comparison tools, 43% omitted payer-specific negotiated rates for at least one major insurer, and 28% contained pricing errors that would produce misleading consumer information.
Price Competition Evidence

Early research on whether price transparency drives competition shows mixed results. Markets with high employer concentration and sophisticated benefit consulting show 4-8% price moderation in shoppable services. Markets with limited insurer competition show no measurable price effect. Consumer-facing price shopping remains rare — fewer than 3% of patients report using hospital price tools before seeking care.

children.text: SDOH Screening Policy Context

The Accountable Health Communities Health-Related Social Needs (AHC-HRSN) screening tool is now required for Medicare and Medicaid beneficiaries in 47 CMS Innovation Center models. Commercial payers including UnitedHealth's Optum and Humana have incorporated SDOH screening into chronic disease management programs. Approximately 34% of U.S. health systems report implementing systematic SDOH screening in clinical workflows.
Screening Performance

Universal SDOH screening completion rates average 61% in health systems with established workflows, with significant variation by care setting: primary care (72%), emergency department (48%), and inpatient (81%). Social need prevalence rates in screened populations: food insecurity (28%), housing instability (19%), transportation barriers (23%), and utility assistance needs (16%).
Referral-to-Resolution Gap

The most significant implementation challenge is the referral-to-resolution gap. Among patients screening positive for social needs, 74% receive a referral to a community resource, but only 31% successfully access the resource within 90 days. Barriers include community resource capacity constraints, navigation complexity, and patient engagement challenges.
Economic Case

HTR's analysis of three published SDOH intervention ROI studies finds a median return of $2.40 per dollar invested in community resource navigation and food security interventions for high-risk Medicaid populations. Returns are concentrated in ED visit reduction and avoidable hospitalization prevention. Payback periods average 18-24 months, requiring payer/provider alignment to capture.

children.text: Documented Bias in Clinical Algorithms

Multiple high-profile studies have documented racial and gender bias in widely deployed clinical algorithms. The Obermeyer et al. (2019) study in Science demonstrated that a commercial risk-stratification algorithm used by major health systems systematically underestimated the severity of illness in Black patients by assigning lower risk scores relative to clinical need — a bias rooted in using healthcare cost as a proxy for health status.
Scope of Affected Algorithms

Documented bias exists across multiple clinical domains: sepsis prediction models underperforming in Black patients (4 of 7 published validations), pain assessment algorithms trained predominantly on white patient data showing reduced accuracy for Asian and Hispanic populations, nephrology eGFR equations (now revised) historically overestimating kidney function in Black patients, and pulmonary function tests using race-based reference equations that may be scientifically unfounded.
Regulatory Framework

HHS Office for Civil Rights has indicated that Section 1557 of the ACA prohibits the use of discriminatory clinical algorithms in covered entities. The 2024 Section 1557 final rule explicitly addresses algorithmic discrimination, requiring health systems to assess AI and decision-support tools for discriminatory impact. Enforcement mechanisms and audit requirements are still being developed.
Mitigation Approaches

Algorithmic bias mitigation requires action at three stages: (1) development — ensuring diverse and representative training datasets, subgroup performance reporting, and fairness constraints in model optimization; (2) validation — mandatory subgroup performance analysis before deployment; and (3) post-market monitoring — ongoing performance surveillance stratified by race, gender, age, and socioeconomic proxies.

children.text: Rural Hospital Closure Trajectory

The Chartis Center for Rural Health documents 147 rural hospital closures since 2010, with an acceleration to 19 closures in 2025 — the highest annual total since 2020. An additional 600+ rural hospitals are classified as financially vulnerable, defined as operating with negative EBITDA margins for two consecutive years.
Geographic Impact

Rural hospital closures concentrate in the South and Midwest, with 10 states accounting for 68% of closures. Counties with hospital closures experience 5.9% increase in cardiovascular mortality, 3.2% increase in maternal mortality, and 11% reduction in local employment within 5 years of closure — impacts that extend far beyond healthcare access.
Workforce Dimension

Rural communities face a compounding challenge: not only are facilities closing, but workforce shortages make reopening or replacing closed services increasingly difficult. Rural areas have 63 primary care physicians per 100,000 residents versus 112 per 100,000 in urban areas. Psychiatry shortage is more severe: 9.3 rural psychiatrists per 100,000 versus 24.1 urban.
Broadband and Telehealth

Federal Communications Commission broadband data shows 19.4M rural Americans lack access to fixed broadband meeting the FCC's 25/3 Mbps threshold — a population that cannot reliably access video telehealth services. The Infrastructure Investment and Jobs Act's $65B broadband investment aims to close this gap by 2030, but construction timelines suggest the coverage gap will persist for 5-7 years.

children.text: Legal Framework

Section 1557 of the ACA prohibits discrimination on the basis of national origin in covered healthcare programs, which HHS interprets to require meaningful access for Limited English Proficient (LEP) patients. Approximately 26M U.S. residents are LEP, including 10.6M who speak Spanish and 9M who speak Asian and Pacific Island languages as their primary language.
Compliance Landscape

A 2025 Joint Commission review of 200 hospitals found 67% had qualified medical interpreter services available 24/7 for the top three languages spoken in their market, but only 29% had such services for the top 10 languages. Telephone interpreter services are available more broadly, but call connection wait times averaged 8.4 minutes — a significant barrier in urgent clinical situations.
Patient Safety Implications

Communication failures in LEP patients are associated with adverse event rates 2-3x higher than English-proficient patients. The most common preventable adverse events include medication errors (wrong dose or frequency conveyed in translation), missed follow-up due to discharge instructions not understood, and delayed diagnosis due to symptom history misinterpretation.

children.text: Community Health Worker Policy Landscape

Community health workers (CHWs) — frontline public health workers who share lived experience with the communities they serve — have emerged as a cost-effective strategy for addressing social determinants and improving health equity. The Affordable Care Act and subsequent state Medicaid expansions have created new reimbursement pathways enabling sustainable CHW employment in clinical settings.
Reimbursement Expansion

As of January 2026, 33 states have authorized Medicaid reimbursement for CHW services under Section 1905(a)(6) of the Social Security Act or through Section 1115 demonstration waivers. Average Medicaid reimbursement for CHW services ranges from $28 to $67 per hour of direct service, with most states requiring physician or advanced practice provider supervision.
Evidence Base

The strongest evidence for CHW effectiveness exists in three domains: diabetes self-management support (average A1c reduction of 0.9 percentage points in six published randomized controlled trials), hypertension control (14% improvement in controlled blood pressure in community-based programs), and maternal health outreach (18% reduction in preterm birth in high-risk populations).
Value-Based Care Integration

CHWs create the most value in two-sided risk contracts where the plan or ACO captures savings from reduced hospitalizations and ED visits. An HTR financial model for a 50,000-member Medicaid ACO shows CHW program ROI of 3.1:1 over three years, with break-even at 22 months assuming full implementation and adequate caseloads of 80-120 active patients per CHW.

children.text: Executive Summary

Vermont's Act 167, signed into law in June 2025, represents the most ambitious state-level health coverage expansion since Massachusetts' 2006 Chapter 58. The legislation requires universal primary care enrollment for all Vermont residents by January 1, 2028, regardless of immigration status or employment.
Legislative Background

The act builds on Vermont's Green Mountain Care Board infrastructure, established under Act 48 (2011). Key provisions include: mandatory enrollment through existing all-payer model networks, a 1.2% payroll surcharge on employers with more than 50 employees, and a federal 1115 waiver application to capture enhanced Medicaid matching funds.
Fiscal Analysis

The Legislative Joint Fiscal Office estimates first-year costs at $340M, rising to $1.2B by Year 3 as the uninsured population is absorbed. The payroll surcharge is projected to generate $280M annually, leaving a structural gap of approximately $920M that requires federal participation.
Federal Waiver Risk

CMS approval of the 1115 waiver is not guaranteed. Vermont's previous waiver application for a global budget (2017) was denied under the prior administration. The current CMS leadership has signaled openness to state flexibility, but has not pre-approved universal primary care models.
Implementation Timeline

Phase 1 (2026): Green Mountain Care Board establishes enrollment infrastructure and contracts with 12 primary care accountable care organizations. Phase 2 (2027): Employer mandate enforcement begins. Phase 3 (2028): Full universal enrollment target.
Analyst Recommendation

States watching Vermont should monitor the CMS waiver outcome closely. If approved, Act 167 creates a replicable model for universal primary care coverage without full single-payer legislation. If denied, Vermont faces a $920M structural deficit that could force program rollback or tax increases.

children.text: The PBM Regulatory Landscape

Pharmacy benefit managers process approximately 80% of U.S. prescription drug claims, yet operate with minimal transparency regarding pricing spreads and rebate flows. The 2025 legislative cycle saw unprecedented state-level action, with 14 states enacting PBM transparency bills and 8 more introducing legislation.
Key Legislative Provisions

The most substantive enacted laws share three core elements: spread pricing prohibition for Medicaid managed care contracts, mandatory rebate pass-through to plan sponsors (typically 85-100%), and annual formulary and network pharmacy disclosure to state insurance commissioners.
Market Impact

Early data from states that enacted PBM transparency laws in 2023-2024 (New York, Ohio, Arkansas) show 12-18% reduction in net drug costs for state employee health plans in the first year. However, PBMs have responded by restructuring fee arrangements to shift from spread to administrative service fees.
Federal Preemption Risk

ERISA preemption remains the primary legal vulnerability for state PBM laws. Self-insured employer plans, which cover approximately 61% of privately insured Americans, are exempt from state insurance regulation under ERISA Section 514. States must structure PBM laws to avoid triggering preemption challenges.

children.text: Scale of the Coverage Loss

Following the end of continuous enrollment protections, states completed redeterminations between April 2023 and December 2024. Final counts show 23.7M individuals lost Medicaid coverage, with 14.8M estimated to be procedurally disenrolled despite remaining eligible — a significant policy failure.

State outcomes varied dramatically. States with ex parte renewal processes and robust data-sharing with unemployment agencies retained 72% of eligible enrollees. children.text: Background on Certificate of Need

Certificate of Need laws, enacted in 36 states and DC, require healthcare providers to obtain state approval before adding beds, acquiring major equipment, or opening new facilities. Originally designed to prevent costly duplication, CON laws have increasingly been criticized for limiting competition and access in underserved markets.
2025-2026 Legislative Activity

The 2025-2026 legislative cycle represents the most active CON reform period in two decades. children.text: The IDR System Collapse

The No Surprises Act (NSA), effective January 2022, was designed to protect patients from unexpected out-of-network bills. Its independent dispute resolution mechanism allows payers and providers to arbitrate payment disputes. The system has been overwhelmed: CMS projected 22,000 annual disputes; actual filings exceeded 700,000 in 2024 alone.
Backlog and Delays

The average dispute resolution time has grown from the statutory 30-day window to 14 months as of Q4 2025. Certified IDR entities, licensed to arbitrate disputes, have struggled to staff adequately. Several entities have withdrawn certification, further concentrating caseload.
Strategic Behavior

Providers — particularly emergency medicine and anesthesiology groups — have used volume IDR filings strategically, anticipating that payers will settle below the qualifying payment amount rather than absorb arbitration costs. Payers have responded by extending network offers to previously non-participating providers to reduce IDR exposure.

children.text: FDA's Evolving AI Regulatory Framework

The FDA has authorized more than 950 AI-enabled medical devices, with the pace of clearances accelerating to 312 in 2024 alone. High-Risk Algorithm Classification

The guidance distinguishes between decision-support software that clinicians are expected to override (lower risk, often exempt from device regulation) and autonomous or locked algorithms driving clinical decisions without independent clinician verification. The latter category faces the most stringent oversight requirements.
Predicate Device Challenge

Novel AI applications in pathology, radiology, and genomics frequently lack adequate predicate devices for 510(k) substantial equivalence. FDA has pushed 47 applications to the De Novo pathway in 2024-2025, a 340% increase from 2022. De Novo authorization typically requires 18-24 months versus 9-12 months for 510(k) clearance.
Post-Market Surveillance

PCCPs require manufacturers to establish performance monitoring protocols across diverse patient populations, with mandatory reporting when algorithm performance degrades below pre-specified thresholds. Early implementations have revealed significant performance drops in non-white patient populations for skin condition detection algorithms.

The Four Structural Barriers

Barrier One is specimen logistics. Genomic testing requires biospecimen collection, preservation, and transport to certified laboratories—a supply chain that assumes same-day courier access. Rural hospitals and clinics frequently lack courier relationships, and patient specimens often sit at room temperature for 24–48 hours, degrading DNA quality and producing inconclusive results that are incorrectly attributed to test quality rather than pre-analytical failures.

Barrier Two is genetics counselor availability. The United States has approximately 5,600 certified genetic counselors; roughly 4% work in settings serving predominantly rural populations. Patients who receive a meaningful genomic test result—a BRCA variant, a pharmacogenomic interaction flag, a hereditary cancer syndrome—require counseling that the rural system cannot provide. Without follow-up, the test result is clinically inert.

Barriers Three and Four are insurance coverage fragmentation and EHR integration deficits. Pharmacogenomic panels, while CMS-reimbursed for certain indications, remain inconsistently covered by Medicaid fee schedules across states, and EHR systems at rural hospitals typically lack the genomic data integration that would allow a clinician to see a pharmacogenomic alert at the point of prescribing.

children.text: Population health management—the discipline of identifying and proactively managing patients with chronic disease risk before they require acute care—has been practiced at urban academic medical centers and large integrated delivery networks for over a decade. Its penetration into rural health systems has been far slower, constrained by the same fragmented EHR infrastructure and limited care coordination staffing that limits every other quality initiative in rural settings.
The Registry Infrastructure: What You Actually Need

The foundational technology for population health management in rural settings does not require a population health platform costing $500,000. Eighty-three percent of the rural health systems with documented outcomes in the published evidence base are running their registries on their existing EHR’s built-in panel management or registry tools. children.text: Risk Stratification Methodologies That Work in Rural Populations

Rural populations present risk stratification challenges that urban-calibrated models handle poorly. The most widely used commercial risk stratification algorithm—the Hierarchical Condition Category (HCC) model—significantly underpredicts risk for rural populations because it underweights transportation barriers and SDOH factors that are highly predictive of rural acute care utilization. Rural systems that have achieved the best outcomes are using augmented HCC models that add SDOH scores and ED utilization history as independent predictors.

The specific SDOH factors with the highest predictive value for rural acute care utilization, based on a 2025 JAMA Internal Medicine analysis of 87,000 rural patients, are: (1) food insecurity (OR 2.8 for 30-day readmission), (2) transportation barrier (OR 2.4), and (3) lack of regular social contact (OR 1.9 for 90-day acute care utilization). These factors are not captured in the HCC model and must be added as data elements.

The HCC model sees a diabetic patient with an HbA1c of 9.2. The augmented rural model sees that same patient—plus the fact that she lives 34 miles from the nearest pharmacy, has no reliable transportation, and eats alone. Those three facts predict her next hospitalization better than the HbA1c.

DATA COLLECTION PRIORITY: Implement a standardized SDOH screening protocol (AHC HRSN screener or PRAPARE) at every primary care encounter. SDOH data is the highest-value addition to a rural risk stratification model and the most commonly missing element in rural EHR infrastructure.

Why Rural Hospitals Are the Preferred Target

Three factors make rural hospitals disproportionately attractive targets. Third, willingness to pay: rural hospitals have demonstrated higher ransom payment rates because they cannot sustain EHR downtime without patient safety consequences and often lack the data backup architecture to restore from backups.

Ransomware groups explicitly target rural hospitals because they know the facility will pay. The combination of critical systems, minimal IT staff, and limited backup capability creates a near-perfect coercion environment.

children.text: The Kaufman Hall National Hospital Flash Report for January 2026 confirms what rural health system analysts have been tracking since mid-2024: the rural hospital financial crisis has entered a new, more acute phase. Forty-three percent of rural hospitals reported negative operating margins in FY 2025, the highest share since the measure was first tracked in 2012 and a 7-point deterioration from FY 2024’s already alarming 36%.
The Three Structural Drivers

The deterioration is driven by three converging pressures. First, labor cost inflation: median rural hospital RN hourly wage increased 18% between 2023 and 2025, while Medicaid rates in most states increased less than 4% over the same period. The gap between input cost inflation and reimbursement growth is the single largest contributor to negative margin expansion.

Second, payer mix erosion: rural counties have experienced disproportionate commercial insurance coverage loss as employers reduce benefit generosity. The share of rural hospital revenue from commercial payers—which subsidize Medicare and Medicaid shortfalls—fell from 31% in 2022 to 27% in 2025. For a $50M rural hospital, this shift represents approximately $2M in lost contribution margin.

Third, volume fragmentation: telehealth expansion and improved transportation have enabled some rural patients to self-select to urban specialty centers for procedures that previously generated revenue for local facilities. Rural hospitals are losing profitable procedural volumes while retaining unprofitable complex and behavioral health volumes.

Despite the aggregate deterioration, 57% of rural hospitals maintained positive operating margins in FY 2025. The rural hospitals that will survive 2026 have already decided what business they are in. The ones that will not have been trying to be everything to everyone with a cost structure built for a different era.

Why Retention Economics Matter More Than Recruitment

The dominant rural workforce strategy has historically focused on recruitment: loan repayment, signing bonuses, and rural training pipelines. A 2025 Robert Wood Johnson Foundation study found that the average all-in cost of replacing a rural RN—including recruitment advertising, agency coverage, orientation, and productivity ramp-up—is $62,000 per departure. Against this figure, retention investments that reduce turnover by even 5 percentage points generate a 4:1 to 6:1 ROI.
Every rural RN who walks out the door costs $62,000 to replace. A $15,000 retention investment that prevents that departure has a 4:1 return. The math is not complicated. The execution is.

Clinical ladder programs with tuition reimbursement address a specific retention vulnerability: the RN who leaves not because of dissatisfaction but because of perceived career ceiling. Rural hospitals that implemented ANCC Pathway to Excellence® programs saw 24–28% reductions in turnover in the first 36 months, with the highest retention effect among the 26–35 age cohort.

Housing subsidies are the retention intervention with the fastest-growing evidence base. Five RHT program states—Vermont, West Virginia, Kentucky, Montana, and New Mexico—have allocated RHT funds specifically for rural clinician housing, reflecting a recognition that the rural workforce crisis is, in part, a real estate crisis in communities where workforce housing has simply not been built.

children.text: The narrative of Vermont's healthcare crisis has long focused on funding models and reimbursement rates, but the underlying mathematical reality is far more brutal: we are running out of people. The state is currently caught in a 'Demographic Pincer' movement. On one side, the demand for high-acuity care is accelerating as the population over 65 is projected to exceed 30% of the total state census by 2040. On the other side, the labor pool capable of delivering that care is evaporating.

This is not merely a recruitment challenge; it is a labor solvency crisis. Data from the Vermont Legislative Research Service and recent workforce assessments indicate a structural deficit that cannot be filled by traditional educational pipelines alone. With a forecasted 13% decline in the working-age population between 2020 and 2030, the state faces a scenario where the ratio of caregivers to patients becomes mathematically unsustainable for rural critical access hospitals.
The Math of Attrition: 1,200 vs. 400

The disparity between supply and demand is stark. The 2024-2026 Vermont Nursing Needs Assessment revealed that the state requires approximately 1,200 new Registered Nurses (RNs) annually to maintain current service levels and replace retiring staff. However, Vermont's educational institutions currently graduate only about 400 RNs per year. This structural gap of 800 nurses annually creates a compounding deficit that disproportionately impacts rural facilities, which lack the brand equity and salary leverage of the UVM Health Network.

We are attempting to fill a leaking bucket with a thimble. When the local educational pipeline supplies only 33% of the necessary replacement rate, rural hospitals are forced to cannibalize each other's staff or turn to the predatory economics of contract labor.

The consequences of this deficit are visible in the operational contraction of rural healthcare. We are witnessing the slow-motion closure of service lines—birthing units, dialysis centers, and psychiatric beds—not because the physical infrastructure is lacking, but because the human infrastructure has eroded. The closure of these units forces patients to travel further for care, increasing the burden on the remaining centralized hubs and further straining their capacity.
The Travel Nurse Dependency Loop

To plug these gaps, Vermont hospitals have become addicted to travel nursing agencies, creating a destructive feedback loop. The economics of travel nursing are essentially a transfer of wealth from non-profit hospital operating margins to private staffing equity. While a staff RN in Vermont might earn an average of $41.38 per hour, travel nurses can command rates upwards of $102 per hour—often working alongside the very staff nurses they out-earn by a factor of 2.5.

children.text: This wage disparity shatters morale and incentivizes local nurses to leave their permanent positions to become travelers themselves, further depleting the core staff. For rural hospitals already operating on razor-thin margins (with 9 out of 14 Vermont hospitals reporting operating losses in 2023), this premium labor cost is catastrophic. It accelerates the depletion of reserves and effectively subsidizes a transient workforce at the expense of long-term community resilience.
Housing as Health Policy

Even if recruitment efforts were perfectly funded, Vermont faces a physical barrier to entry: housing. The acute shortage of affordable housing in rural Vermont acts as a hard cap on workforce expansion. Hospital recruiters frequently report candidates accepting offers, only to withdraw them weeks later after failing to find a place to live within a reasonable commuting distance.

This intersection of housing and health policy is critical. Without a coordinated strategy to develop workforce housing specifically for healthcare professionals, salary incentives are rendered ineffective. The '13% workforce decline' is not just about age; it is about the inability of younger families to physically enter the Vermont economic ecosystem. Until housing is treated as a component of the healthcare infrastructure, the vacancy rates in rural nursing will remain stubbornly high.

children.text: The CDC’s December 2025 Rural-Urban Health Disparities Surveillance Report presents a picture that defies simple characterization. Aggregate rural-urban health outcome gaps—measured by age-adjusted mortality, preventable hospitalization rates, and chronic disease control—have improved modestly since 2020 in some categories and deteriorated sharply in others. Understanding the divergence is essential for allocating the limited clinical and financial resources available for rural health equity investment.
Where Gaps Are Narrowing

Cardiovascular disease mortality is the clearest positive trend. The rural-urban age-adjusted cardiovascular mortality gap has narrowed from 37% in 2019 to 28% in 2024, driven by three parallel forces: improved telehealth access for cardiac monitoring and medication management, the expansion of CAH cardiac rehabilitation programs supported by RHT infrastructure funding, and improved statin and antihypertensive medication adherence enabled by community pharmacy expansion in rural markets.

Cancer screening rates show improvement in colorectal and cervical cancer, with the rural-urban gap narrowing 8–12 percentage points since 2020. Mobile screening unit deployment—a strategy adopted by 14 state RHT programs—is the primary driver, with each additional mobile unit estimated to close approximately 3–4% of the rural-urban screening gap in its service area over 24 months.

body.title: Rural-Urban Health Outcome Gap Trends: 2019–2024

children.text: Where Gaps Are Widening: The Three Crisis Categories

Maternal mortality is the most alarming widening disparity. The rural maternal mortality rate reached 61% above the urban rate in 2024—up from 48% in 2019—driven by a combination of obstetric unit closures (86 rural hospitals lost their OB units between 2020 and 2024), worsening hemorrhage management capability at rural EDs receiving transferred patients, and deteriorating postpartum follow-up rates as rural primary care capacity has shrunk.

The rural mental health and suicide mortality gap has widened from 74% to 89% above urban rates over the same period, reflecting both the absolute shortage of rural mental health providers and the failure of telehealth expansion to fully compensate for the loss of community mental health center capacity in rural markets. Rural counties with no licensed mental health provider within 30 miles—now numbering 1,242—show the steepest deterioration.

The maternal mortality data is not a slow-moving trend we can plan around. A 61% rural premium means that a woman giving birth in rural Georgia faces dramatically higher mortality risk than her urban counterpart. This is a measurable, preventable, ongoing harm.

INVESTMENT PRIORITY: The evidence base is clear that the three widening disparity categories—maternal mortality, mental health, and SUD—require targeted direct investment, not general rural health system improvement. Programs that improve average rural health outcomes without specifically targeting these categories will not bend the mortality curve on the indicators that matter most.

children.text: The debate over full-practice authority (FPA) for nurse practitioners and, increasingly, physician assistants, has moved from professional turf to empirical policy evaluation. With 27 states and D.C. now granting NPs FPA, a decade of implementation evidence allows researchers to distinguish the conditions under which scope expansion actually closes access gaps from those in which it produces minimal change.
The Access Improvement Evidence Base

A 2025 Health Affairs meta-analysis of 14 studies across FPA and non-FPA states found a statistically significant but geographically concentrated access improvement: the average FPA state saw a 12% increase in NP-provided primary care visits in rural Health Professional Shortage Areas in the first three years post-enactment. However, two-thirds of that improvement was concentrated in states that paired FPA with Medicaid reimbursement parity—states that granted FPA without parity showed no statistically significant access change.
Full-practice authority without Medicaid reimbursement parity is a permission slip without a paycheck. The access gains only materialize when NPs can build financially viable independent practices.

children.text: CMS’s 2024 Quality Payment Program updates added SDOH screening rates to the Merit-based Incentive Payment System (MIPS) measure set, creating a financial incentive for rural practices to document social needs screening. The predictable result has been a surge in screening rates accompanied by minimal change in patient outcomes: rural practices are asking the PRAPARE or AHC HRSN questions, documenting the responses, and then doing nothing with the data because no referral infrastructure exists.
The Closed-Loop Referral Network: What Separates Effective From Performative SDOH Programs

The defining characteristic of SDOH programs that generate clinical outcomes is the closed-loop referral: a workflow in which a positive SDOH screen automatically generates a referral to a community resource, and the referral system tracks completion and feeds resolution data back to the clinical team. Without the feedback loop, a positive food insecurity screen that generates a referral to a food pantry the patient never contacts is indistinguishable—in the clinical record—from a referral that resulted in three months of regular food access.

children.text: Four Rural Health Systems That Built It

Carilion Clinic (Virginia) partnered with Unite Us to build a closed-loop referral network across seven rural counties. In the first 18 months, 62% of referred patients received a community service within 30 days, and the cohort showed a 16% reduction in ED utilization compared to matched controls. The investment was $280,000 in the first year (Unite Us licensing, care coordinator training, community organization onboarding).

CHAP’s rural network in Appalachian Kentucky embedded community health workers—rather than software platforms—as the referral mechanism. CHWs with deep community relationships achieved 71% referral completion rates and generated an average $3,400 reduction in 12-month care costs per enrolled patient with multiple SDOH needs. The labor model (CHW salary: $38,000–48,000) is accessible to rural systems that cannot afford enterprise SDOH platforms.

The technology is the easy part. A food pantry that does not have capacity to absorb 200 new patients does not become more capable because you build an elegant referral interface. The network is the hard part.

NETWORK BUILDING PRIORITY: Before selecting an SDOH technology platform, conduct a community resource capacity audit. Map the actual service capacity of every organization in your referral network. A closed-loop system that routes patients to over-capacity organizations will generate lower completion rates than a manual system with a well-resourced CHW.

children.text: Imagine you want to start a new kind of restaurant — one that charges customers a flat monthly fee to eat as many healthy meals as they need, rather than charging per dish. The idea makes sense nutritionally and economically. But before you open, you discover that local zoning laws require all food establishments to post per-item prices. The health department’s inspection checklist was designed for traditional menus. Your liquor license application has no category for subscription dining. None of these rules were written to block your idea — they were simply written when your idea did not exist. This is precisely the situation that value-based care innovators face in the American healthcare regulatory environment. The laws, billing codes, anti-kickback rules, and licensure frameworks that govern U.S. healthcare were almost entirely written for a fee-for-service world. Navigating, modifying, and sometimes working around them is not a bureaucratic inconvenience for VBC implementation — it is one of its defining challenges.
Why Policy Is a Pillar, Not Just a Background Condition

Healthcare is one of the most heavily regulated industries in the United States, and for good reason: the decisions made in healthcare settings involve life and death, profound information asymmetry between providers and patients, and the expenditure of trillions of dollars of public funds. The regulatory architecture that governs healthcare payment — Medicare and Medicaid rules, anti-kickback statutes, the Stark Law governing physician self-referral, state insurance laws, and HIPAA privacy regulations — was built incrementally over six decades, each layer added in response to a specific problem or abuse. The result is a regulatory environment of extraordinary complexity that can simultaneously protect patients and obstruct innovation, often in the same rule. For value-based care specifically, the policy environment matters in three distinct ways: it determines which VBC models are legally permissible, it shapes the financial terms under which VBC contracts can operate, and it establishes the data sharing authorities that VBC’s information infrastructure depends upon.

The good news for learners approaching this material is that you do not need to become a healthcare attorney to understand the policy landscape for VBC. What you do need is a working knowledge of four things: the major federal legislation that authorized and funds VBC programs, the agency — CMS and its Innovation Center — that designs and operates most federal VBC models, the specific legal waivers that allow VBC arrangements to operate outside standard fee-for-service rules, and the state-level Medicaid policy environment that governs VBC adoption for the Medicaid population, which represents 22% of all U.S. healthcare spending and the majority of payer mix for rural and safety-net hospitals. This module covers all four in sequence, with enough practical depth that you can apply the concepts to your organization’s specific situation.
The ACA’s Innovation Center: The Engine of U.S. VBC Development

The Center for Medicare and Medicaid Innovation, universally known as CMMI, was established by Section 3021 of the Affordable Care Act in 2010 with a mandatory appropriation of $10 billion over ten years and a statutory mission to test, evaluate, and scale new payment and delivery models that reduce spending while preserving or improving quality. CMMI’s legal authority is significant: it can implement new payment models for Medicare and Medicaid without going through the standard notice-and-comment rulemaking process that governs most federal regulation, as long as the model operates within specific statutory parameters and is evaluated by CMS’s Office of the Actuary. This streamlined authority was deliberately designed to allow rapid policy experimentation — the legislative drafters recognized that VBC model design requires iteration and learning, and that subjecting every model modification to a 12-month rulemaking cycle would make meaningful innovation impossible.

Since 2011, CMMI has launched more than 50 distinct payment model pilots across Medicare and Medicaid, covering primary care transformation, specialty care bundling, accountable care organizations, direct contracting, and state-level all-payer models. The budget allocated per model varies enormously — from small demonstration projects covering a few thousand beneficiaries to large-scale national programs like the Medicare Shared Savings Program, which enrolled 11.2 million beneficiaries by 2025. CMMI’s mandate requires it to demonstrate that each model either reduces net Medicare spending, improves quality without increasing spending, or both. Models that fail to meet these thresholds are terminated. As of 2025, CMMI has terminated 14 models for insufficient evidence of savings or quality improvement, a track record that reflects honest evaluation but has also generated criticism from providers who invested substantially in model infrastructure before termination decisions.

CMMI’s authority to move faster than the standard rulemaking process is its most valuable feature and its most politically contested one. Every model CMMI launches is a hypothesis about how to organize care better. Some hypotheses are wrong. The question is whether the system is learning fast enough from both successes and failures. — Dr. Rahul Rajkumar, former CMMI Deputy Director, Health Affairs Blog, 2024.
MACRA: The Law That Made VBC Participation Effectively Mandatory for Physicians

If CMMI is the engine of federal VBC development, the Medicare Access and CHIP Reauthorization Act of 2015 — universally known as MACRA — is the law that turned VBC from an optional experiment into the default trajectory for physician payment in Medicare. MACRA was passed with rare bipartisan consensus, repealing the deeply unpopular Sustainable Growth Rate formula that had governed Medicare physician payments since 1997 and replacing it with a two-track system that explicitly links physician payment updates to VBC participation. Understanding MACRA’s structure is essential for any clinical or administrative leader whose organization bills Medicare for physician services, because it directly determines how physicians are paid and how much.

MACRA’s two tracks work as follows. Physicians who remain in traditional fee-for-service Medicare participate in the Merit-based Incentive Payment System, or MIPS, which adjusts their annual Medicare payments up or down by up to 9% based on performance across four categories: quality (45% weight), promoting interoperability (25%), improvement activities (15%), and cost (15%). MIPS is designed as a transitional step — it maintains the fee-for-service base payment structure while adding a performance overlay that rewards quality and penalizes inefficiency. The alternative track, and the one that MACRA’s architects intended as the destination, is participation in an Advanced Alternative Payment Model, or APM, which includes CMS-approved VBC arrangements that meet specific risk and quality criteria. Physicians who generate a sufficient share of their Medicare revenue through APM participation receive a 5% lump-sum bonus payment and are exempt from MIPS reporting requirements — a substantial financial incentive to move toward more advanced VBC structures.
The MIPS-to-APM Progression: What It Looks Like in Practice

The practical effect of MACRA’s two-track architecture is to create a structured pathway from fee-for-service through MIPS participation toward Advanced APM engagement, with financial incentives escalating at each stage. A solo primary care physician in rural Wyoming who bills Medicare exclusively on a fee-for-service basis is automatically enrolled in MIPS and will receive payment adjustments — upward or downward — based on their quality reporting, EHR utilization, and cost performance. The same physician who joins a CMMI-approved Accountable Care Organization and generates 50% of their Medicare revenue through that ACO qualifies as an Advanced APM participant, receives the 5% bonus, and escapes the MIPS reporting burden. MACRA’s architecture was designed to make this progression financially attractive enough that providers would voluntarily move toward advanced VBC structures over time, without the political controversy of making VBC participation legally mandatory.

children.text: Policy Insight for Practice Leaders: If your organization’s physicians are currently in MIPS and scoring below 75, you are almost certainly paying more in administrative reporting costs than you are receiving in payment bonuses. The CMS data consistently shows that the cost of MIPS compliance for small and independent practices averages $12,800 per physician per year in staff time and technology costs. Joining an ACO or Advanced APM eliminates this burden while generating shared savings upside. The question is not whether to make the move — it is when your organization has the infrastructure to do it responsibly.
The Stark Law and Anti-Kickback Statute: The Rules VBC Had to Work Around

Two of the most significant legal barriers to value-based care adoption are laws that were designed to protect patients from fraud: the Stark Law, which prohibits physician self-referral for designated health services when a financial relationship exists between the physician and the referred entity, and the Federal Anti-Kickback Statute, which prohibits offering or receiving anything of value to induce referrals of federal healthcare program business. Both laws were enacted in the 1980s and 1990s to address genuine abuses in fee-for-service medicine — physicians referring patients to laboratories or imaging centers they owned, and pharmaceutical companies paying physicians to prescribe specific drugs. They are important protections. They are also written in a way that, on their face, makes many value-based care arrangements technically illegal.

Consider a simple VBC arrangement: a hospital wants to share a portion of the savings generated by an ACO with the primary care physicians who successfully manage their attributed patient panels and reduce unnecessary hospitalizations. Under a strict reading of the Anti-Kickback Statute, this payment could be characterized as remuneration to physicians for reducing referrals to the hospital — which is exactly what the statute was written to prohibit when the financial relationship runs in the other direction. In November 2020, CMS and the Department of Justice’s Office of Inspector General simultaneously published new rules — commonly called the Stark Law and AKS VBC Exceptions — that created explicit regulatory safe harbors for value-based arrangements meeting specific criteria. These exceptions are the legal foundation on which most current VBC contract structures rest, and understanding their existence (if not their full technical detail) is important context for any leader involved in VBC contract negotiation.
What the 2020 VBC Exceptions Actually Allow

The 2020 Stark Law and AKS VBC exceptions created three tiers of safe harbor protection based on the level of financial risk the arrangement assumes. The first tier, the “care coordination arrangement” exception, covers low-risk VBC arrangements where physicians and hospitals share non-monetary resources — care coordinators, technology platforms, data analytics tools — without direct financial remuneration flowing between them. The second tier covers arrangements where the parties share substantial downside financial risk, defined as the physician group being responsible for a meaningful share of losses if spending targets are not met. The third and most protective tier applies to arrangements where a physician entity is “fully at risk” — accepting capitation-level accountability for a defined patient population. The practical effect of this tiered structure is that more financially protective exceptions are available to VBC arrangements that accept more financial risk — a policy design that explicitly incentivizes providers to move toward more advanced VBC models in exchange for greater legal certainty.
State Medicaid Policy: Where VBC Gets Complicated Fast

Medicaid, the joint federal-state health insurance program for low-income Americans, covers 90 million people and represents 22% of all U.S. healthcare spending. For rural and safety-net hospitals, Medicaid is often the dominant payer — in some Critical Access Hospitals, Medicaid accounts for more than 40% of patient volume. Any serious discussion of VBC adoption must therefore grapple with Medicaid policy, and Medicaid policy is, by design, a state-level affair. Under the Social Security Act, the federal government sets minimum Medicaid standards and matches state spending at rates ranging from 50% to 90% depending on state per-capita income — but states have substantial flexibility in how they design their Medicaid programs, including how they pay providers. This flexibility has produced a 50-state patchwork of Medicaid VBC approaches that range from nationally leading to years behind, often with little correlation to state wealth or healthcare system capacity.

States access this flexibility primarily through two mechanisms: Section 1115 waivers, which allow states to use Medicaid funds in ways not otherwise permitted by federal statute in exchange for CMS approval of a formal waiver application and evaluation framework, and Section 1915 waivers, which allow states to require Medicaid beneficiaries to enroll in managed care organizations rather than traditional fee-for-service Medicaid. As of 2025, 41 states operate Medicaid managed care programs covering at least some beneficiary populations, and 24 states have active Section 1115 waivers that include VBC-oriented payment reform components. The remaining states continue to operate primarily fee-for-service Medicaid programs, creating a two-tier national Medicaid environment where the VBC infrastructure, data systems, and provider capabilities in a given state depend heavily on decisions made by state legislatures and Medicaid agencies that most healthcare professionals are only vaguely aware of.
