children.text: The state variation in Medicaid VBC adoption documented in the table above is not simply a story of some states moving faster than others. It reflects fundamentally different political economies, administrative capacities, and provider infrastructure realities. Massachusetts’ MassHealth ACO Program, which places 78% of Medicaid beneficiaries in global budget arrangements, required a decade of incremental managed care development, a sophisticated state health information exchange, and a robust community health worker infrastructure before global budgets were feasible. Mississippi, which remains 89% fee-for-service Medicaid, faces not just a political environment less favorable to managed care but a provider infrastructure so financially fragile — as examined in the DSH module — that asking rural hospitals to accept downside financial risk before their basic solvency is secured would be policy malpractice. Understanding this context prevents the common mistake of treating state VBC laggards as simply lacking political will, when the more accurate diagnosis is often a missing infrastructure foundation.
The AHEAD Model: The Boldest Current Federal VBC Policy Experiment

The CMS All-Payer Health Equity Approaches and Development Model, known as AHEAD, launched in 2023 and represents the most ambitious federal VBC policy experiment currently active in the United States. AHEAD is fundamentally different from previous CMS models in one critical way: it operates across all payers simultaneously, not just Medicare. In the eight participating states — Maryland, Vermont, Connecticut, Hawaii, Minnesota, New York, Rhode Island, and Washington — CMS is working with state governments and commercial insurers to establish coordinated spending targets that apply to Medicare, Medicaid, and commercial insurance simultaneously. The goal is to eliminate the perverse incentive created by single-payer VBC models, where a provider that successfully reduces costs for its Medicare ACO population may simply shift utilization to its commercially insured population, producing savings for Medicare at the expense of commercial payer spending.

AHEAD’s architecture has three components that build on each other. Hospital Global Budgets establish annual spending targets for inpatient and outpatient hospital care, similar to the model Maryland has operated since 1977 under a waiver from standard Medicare payment rules. Primary Care Investment establishes a per-capita funding floor for primary care services in each participating state, addressing the underfunding of primary care that Module 1 identified as a structural driver of the U.S. spending-outcomes gap. And the Health Equity Plan requires each participating state to establish specific, measurable goals for reducing health outcome disparities across racial, ethnic, geographic, and socioeconomic dimensions, with CMS oversight of progress toward those goals as a condition of continued model participation. AHEAD’s early results will not be statistically meaningful until 2027 at the earliest, but its structural design represents the most coherent attempt yet to address the whole-system payment reform that health economists have argued is necessary for genuine transformation.

The AHEAD Model is not a pilot. It is a policy architecture for what the American healthcare payment system could look like at scale — one where no payer is an island, where primary care is funded as infrastructure rather than as a commodity, and where health equity is a contractual obligation rather than an aspiration. Whether it works depends entirely on whether the participating states build the administrative and data infrastructure to make the targets meaningful. — HTR Regulatory Intelligence Assessment, Q1 2026.
Reading Policy Signals: How to Know What’s Coming Before It Arrives

One of the most practical skills a healthcare leader can develop is the ability to read federal policy signals early — to understand what CMS, Congress, and state Medicaid agencies are signaling about the future direction of payment policy before new rules take effect. This skill is valuable because VBC model participation requires organizational investment — in data systems, care management staffing, and actuarial capabilities — that takes 18 to 36 months to build. Organizations that wait until a rule is finalized to begin building readiness will always be behind. The following framework identifies the primary signals that healthcare leaders should monitor continuously as leading indicators of VBC policy direction.

CMS Requests for Information (RFIs) are formal public notices in which CMS invites stakeholder comment on a policy concept before publishing a proposed rule. An RFI on a new payment model concept typically precedes a proposed rule by 12–18 months, giving organizations that monitor them a substantial head start on understanding what is coming and beginning internal readiness assessments.

The Annual Physician Fee Schedule Proposed Rule, published every July for the following calendar year, contains the annual MIPS threshold adjustments, quality measure updates, and any modifications to Advanced APM qualifying criteria. Reading the proposed rule summary — not the full document, which runs to thousands of pages — each July is the single most efficient way to stay current on federal physician payment policy.

CMMI Model Termination Notices are official signals that a payment model has not met its statutory savings or quality thresholds. When CMMI terminates a model, it typically publishes evaluation findings that explain why. Reading these findings is often more instructive than reading the original model design documents, because they identify the specific infrastructure gaps, attribution problems, or market conditions that prevented the model from working — lessons directly applicable to understanding what makes other VBC models succeed.

State Medicaid Managed Care Request for Proposals are published by state Medicaid agencies when they are procuring new managed care contracts, typically on three-to-five year cycles. These documents specify the quality metrics, VBC incentive structures, SDOH screening requirements, and health equity goals that Medicaid managed care organizations and their provider networks will be held to. Organizations that serve Medicaid populations should read their state’s current managed care RFP as a direct statement of the performance expectations they will face in the next contract cycle.
Module 2 Summary: The Policy Environment Is Not Your Enemy — But You Must Understand It

The policy architecture governing value-based care in the United States is complex, layered, and still evolving — but it is not impenetrable to practitioners willing to invest in understanding its structure. The key institutions are CMS and its Innovation Center, which design and operate most federal VBC models; Congress, which authorizes and funds VBC infrastructure through legislation like MACRA and the ACA; and state Medicaid agencies, which determine how value-based principles are applied to the Medicaid population that drives solvency for most safety-net and rural providers. The key legal frameworks are MACRA’s two-track physician payment architecture, the 2020 Stark Law and Anti-Kickback VBC exceptions, and the Section 1115 and 1915 waiver authorities that give states flexibility to innovate within federal Medicaid rules.

The most important single insight from this module is that policy does not just regulate VBC — it enables it. The shared savings that MSSP ACOs distribute to physicians are legal because of CMMI’s model authority and the AKS safe harbor. The global budgets that Maryland hospitals operate under are legal because of a 47-year-old CMS waiver. The care coordination resources that a hospital shares with its independent physician partners are legally protected because of the 2020 VBC exceptions. Every advanced VBC arrangement you will encounter in your career rests on a specific legal and regulatory foundation. Understanding that foundation — at least at the level of knowing which questions to ask your legal team — is not optional for any leader who wants to move their organization toward value.

Identify your organization’s current MACRA track: are your physicians primarily in MIPS, in an Advanced APM, or in both? If primarily MIPS, what is the organization’s target timeline for APM qualification, and what infrastructure gaps stand between you and that threshold?

Review your state’s current Medicaid managed care contract or RFP. Identify the three quality metrics with the highest incentive weight and assess your organization’s current performance on each. The gap between your current performance and the contract’s quality bonus threshold is a direct measure of revenue at risk.

Determine whether your state is an AHEAD Model participant. If yes, begin engaging your state hospital association and state health department about the hospital global budget timeline and what data your organization will need to submit. If no, monitor CMS for the next AHEAD cohort solicitation, expected in late 2026.

Schedule a conversation with your legal or compliance team specifically about the 2020 Stark Law and Anti-Kickback VBC exceptions. Ask them to identify any current or planned VBC arrangements at your organization that rely on these exceptions, and to confirm that the arrangements are structured to satisfy the applicable safe harbor criteria.

Module 2 Key Takeaway: The U.S. healthcare policy environment was built for fee-for-service, but it has been systematically modified over the past 15 years to enable value-based care. CMMI’s model authority, MACRA’s APM incentive structure, the 2020 VBC legal exceptions, and state Medicaid waiver programs together constitute a policy architecture that makes advanced VBC legally and financially feasible for most U.S. healthcare organizations. The organizations that understand this architecture and align their strategy to it are the ones that will be best positioned as CMS accelerates its stated goal of having 100% of Medicare beneficiaries in an accountable care relationship by 2030.

children.text: Here is a question that sounds simple but is genuinely hard to answer: if a hospital successfully reduces its patients’ hospitalization rate by 15% through better care management, is that good news or bad news for the hospital’s finances? The instinctive answer is that it must be good news — fewer hospitalizations means healthier patients, which is surely the goal. But in a world where 40% of that hospital’s revenue still comes from fee-for-service Medicare and Medicaid payments, fewer hospitalizations means fewer inpatient admissions, which means fewer billed days, which means lower revenue. The hospital just cut its own income by doing its job better. This is not a hypothetical paradox — it is the central economic tension of the volume-to-value transition, experienced by virtually every health system that has seriously engaged with value-based care. Understanding this tension, and the financial mechanisms that VBC contract structures use to resolve it, is what this module is about.
The Financial Anatomy of a Shared Savings Contract

The Medicare Shared Savings Program is the most widely adopted VBC model in the United States, and shared savings is the financial mechanism at its core. Understanding how shared savings actually works — how the benchmark is set, how savings are calculated, and how they are distributed — is the foundation for understanding the economics of most VBC arrangements. The concept is straightforward: CMS calculates how much it would have expected to spend on your attributed patient population if they had remained in traditional fee-for-service Medicare, adjusted for their age, health status, and geographic cost factors. This projected spend is your “benchmark.” If your ACO’s actual spending on that population comes in below the benchmark, the difference is “savings.” You share those savings with CMS according to a pre-agreed formula — typically retaining 40–75% depending on your risk track and quality performance, with CMS keeping the remainder.

The devil, as always, is in the details. The benchmark calculation uses a three-year historical average of your patient population’s spending, adjusted upward by a national trend factor. For ACOs whose patient populations were already low-cost before joining the program, this creates an immediate structural problem: their benchmark is low, so even excellent care management produces modest absolute savings, making the shared savings payment insufficient to cover the care management infrastructure investment. This is called the “low benchmark problem,” and it is the primary reason that rural and safety-net ACOs, which often already operate lean systems with lower baseline utilization, struggle to generate shared savings large enough to justify Advanced APM participation costs. CMS has modified the benchmark methodology three times since 2012 in response to this problem, most recently in the Pathways to Success Rule of 2018 and the 2023 ACO Primary Care Flex Model, but the fundamental tension between historical benchmarking and equitable VBC participation for already-efficient providers remains unresolved.
Upside-Only vs. Two-Sided Risk: The Decision That Changes Everything

One of the most consequential decisions a provider organization makes when entering a shared savings arrangement is whether to accept only upside risk — where you share in savings if you beat the benchmark but owe nothing if you miss it — or two-sided risk, where you both share savings and repay losses if spending exceeds the benchmark. This choice has profound implications for the financial planning, working capital requirements, and organizational risk appetite of the participating entity. Upside-only arrangements (MSSP Track 1 and its successors) are appropriate for organizations beginning their VBC journey: they provide financial experience with population cost management without the catastrophic downside scenario of a major loss repayment obligation. Two-sided arrangements (MSSP ENHANCED Track, Direct Contracting, ACO REACH) offer higher shared savings percentages — sometimes up to 80% of savings — but require the organization to maintain actuarial reserves sufficient to cover a loss scenario, typically modeled at 1–3% of benchmark spending.

children.text: The financial model in the table above illustrates why Two-Sided and Full-Risk tracks are substantially more attractive in their best-case financial outcome — but also why the actuarial reserve requirement creates a genuine barrier to entry for organizations operating at thin margins. For a health system with $30 million in unrestricted net assets, maintaining a $2.5 million actuarial reserve for ACO REACH participation represents a 8.3% allocation of available capital to a risk management buffer — a rational investment if leadership has high confidence in the organization’s ability to manage population cost, but a significant commitment that requires board-level approval and careful opportunity cost analysis against other capital needs.
Bundled Payments: When a Single Price Covers an Entire Episode of Care

Bundled payment models take a different economic approach to aligning incentives than shared savings. Rather than holding a provider accountable for the total cost of care across an entire attributed population, bundled payments establish a single target price for all the care associated with a specific clinical episode — typically defined as a procedure or hospitalization plus 90 days of post-acute care. If the sum of all actual payments during the episode falls below the target price, the lead provider (typically the hospital or physician group that performed the primary procedure) retains the difference. If actual costs exceed the target, the lead provider repays the excess. The economic logic is straightforward: bundled payments create a direct financial incentive for the hospital performing a hip replacement to care about which skilled nursing facility the patient is discharged to, how long they stay there, and whether they end up readmitted — because all of those costs are included in the bundle.

BPCI Advanced, CMS’s current bundled payment program, covers 32 clinical episodes ranging from major joint replacement and cardiac surgery to pneumonia and chronic obstructive pulmonary disease hospitalizations. The program has generated the strongest evidence of any CMS alternative payment model for procedural episodes: a 2024 CMS evaluation found that BPCI Advanced participants reduced episode spending by an average of $2,100 per episode for major joint replacement while maintaining or improving quality outcomes, generating net Medicare savings of $900 million between 2018 and 2023. Critically, these savings came primarily from reductions in post-acute care spending — fewer days in skilled nursing facilities and more patients discharged directly home with home health services — rather than from reductions in the procedural care itself, confirming the bundled payment hypothesis that the primary driver of unnecessary cost in high-volume procedures is the post-acute care tail, not the procedure.

The bundled payment evidence for joint replacement is about as clean as healthcare economics gets: when you make the hospital financially responsible for what happens after the patient leaves, patients spend less time in nursing homes, have fewer complications, and cost Medicare significantly less money. The same logic applies to any high-volume procedure with a predictable post-acute care pattern. The challenge is applying it to medical conditions where the post-acute trajectory is far less predictable. — Leemore Dafny, Harvard Business School, Health Affairs, 2025.
Capitation: The Most Advanced — and Most Misunderstood — VBC Model

Capitation is the payment model that most completely aligns provider incentives with patient health outcomes, and the one that generates the most anxiety among providers who have not operated under it before. Under capitation, a provider or provider organization receives a fixed payment per enrolled member per month — the “PMPM” rate — and is responsible for delivering or arranging all covered healthcare services for that member, regardless of how much care they actually use. If the member uses more care than the PMPM covers, the provider absorbs the loss. If the member uses less, the provider retains the surplus. This structure creates the strongest possible financial incentive for prevention, care coordination, and early intervention — because every avoided hospitalization translates directly into retained revenue rather than lost fee-for-service income.

The anxiety around capitation is understandable but often misdirected. The concern most commonly expressed is that capitation incentivizes providers to withhold necessary care — to under-treat rather than over-treat. This concern is real and has historical basis: the managed care capitation models of the 1990s were frequently criticized for exactly this failure, and some HMO capitation arrangements did produce documented under-treatment in specific service categories. But the lesson of the 1990s HMO experience is not that capitation is inherently dangerous. It is that capitation without robust quality measurement, meaningful patient choice, and strong external accountability produces dangerous incentives. Modern capitation models — including Medicare Advantage plans and CMS’s ACO REACH program — include comprehensive quality metric frameworks with financial consequences for poor performance, minimum coverage requirements that prevent service restriction below evidence-based thresholds, and beneficiary rights to seek care outside the network when needed. The capitation model that exists in 2026 is substantively different from the managed care capitation of 1996.
How PMPM Rates Are Set: The Actuarial Core of Capitation

The financial success or failure of a capitation arrangement is largely determined before any patient is seen, at the point where the PMPM rate is negotiated or set. If the rate is set too low relative to the actual cost of providing care to the enrolled population, no amount of care management efficiency will produce a viable financial model. If the rate is set appropriately — reflecting the health acuity, demographic profile, and social complexity of the enrolled population — a well-managed capitated provider can generate margins of 3–8% while delivering care that is demonstrably better in quality and lower in total cost than the fee-for-service alternative. The actuarial process of setting a PMPM rate involves risk adjustment models that account for enrollee diagnoses, functional status, and social determinants of health, applied to utilization cost data from comparable populations. For Medicare Advantage plans, CMS sets the base rate using the county-level fee-for-service benchmark and adjusts it upward or downward based on each enrollee’s Hierarchical Condition Category (HCC) risk score, a diagnosis-based model that attempts to predict expected healthcare utilization for that individual in the coming year.
The Volume-to-Value Transition: Why the Math Gets Hard Before It Gets Easy

The single most common financial mistake health systems make in VBC transitions is underestimating the revenue disruption of the transition period — the window, typically 18 to 36 months, during which care management investments have begun reducing utilization but VBC contract revenue has not yet scaled to replace the lost fee-for-service volume. Consider a regional health system generating $400 million in annual net patient revenue, with 30% of that revenue from inpatient admissions billed on a fee-for-service basis. The system joins MSSP and invests $2 million in care management infrastructure — care coordinators, a risk stratification platform, a post-discharge follow-up program — that begins generating measurable results in year one, reducing its attributed Medicare population’s hospitalization rate by 12%. That 12% reduction represents approximately 240 avoided admissions. At an average net revenue of $8,500 per admission, it also represents a $2.04 million reduction in fee-for-service inpatient revenue. The system’s MSSP shared savings payment for year one, based on total population savings, might be $1.4 million. Net financial impact of year one VBC investment: negative $640,000.

This math is not an argument against VBC. It is an argument for understanding VBC as a multi-year financial investment with a specific payback horizon, rather than a year-one revenue enhancement strategy. The financial literature on mature ACO performance consistently shows that organizations reaching their fifth year of MSSP participation generate shared savings payments averaging $312 per attributed beneficiary annually, compared to an average investment cost of $87 per beneficiary in care management infrastructure — a return on investment of approximately 3.6 to 1. The problem is that most health system financial planning cycles operate on one-to-three year horizons, which are too short to capture the full economic benefit of VBC investment. Organizations that have successfully navigated the volume-to-value transition have done so by securing board approval for a five-to-seven year VBC investment thesis with explicit transition period loss projections, rather than attempting to justify each year’s VBC expenditure against that same year’s VBC revenue.

For CFOs and Finance Leaders: If your organization is evaluating ACO or Advanced APM participation, your financial model must explicitly project the transition period revenue displacement — the reduction in fee-for-service inpatient and ED revenue that will occur as care management succeeds. An ACO financial model that shows positive net revenue in year one almost certainly has a methodology error, either in the care management cost estimates or in the assumed savings rate. Realistic five-year models typically show a cumulative loss in years one and two, breakeven in year three, and meaningful positive return in years four and five. Present this model honestly to your board, or the VBC investment will be defunded the first time a quarterly loss appears.
Primary Care Investment as Economic Infrastructure

One of the most powerful and counterintuitive findings in health economics is that investment in primary care produces returns that are comparable to, and in many cases superior to, investment in specialty care infrastructure — not in terms of individual clinical case intensity, but in terms of total population health spending and outcomes. The economic mechanism is straightforward once articulated: primary care reduces the incidence of the expensive downstream events — hospitalizations, emergency visits, specialist procedures, complications of uncontrolled chronic disease — that account for the vast majority of total healthcare spending. A study published in Health Affairs in 2024 analyzing Medicare spending patterns across 306 hospital referral regions found that regions with above-median primary care physician supply had 11.2% lower total Medicare spending per beneficiary, 18.4% fewer preventable hospital admissions, and 14.7% lower 30-day readmission rates than regions with below-median primary care supply, after controlling for demographic and health status differences.

The economic return on primary care investment is particularly relevant for value-based care organizations making resource allocation decisions. Under fee-for-service, a hospital has limited financial incentive to invest in expanding primary care capacity in its community — more primary care visits may mean fewer specialist referrals and fewer hospitalizations, which means less hospital revenue. Under a capitated or shared savings VBC model, the same investment in primary care capacity is a direct cost reduction strategy: every diabetic patient who sees their primary care provider quarterly and maintains target HbA1c levels is a patient who is unlikely to generate an $18,000 diabetic complication admission. The VBC payment model converts primary care from a cost center competing with hospital services for capital allocation into a return-generating infrastructure investment — which is the single most important realignment that value-based payment architecture produces.

children.text: The ROI data in the table above carries an important caveat: these are population-level averages from mature ACOs that have already built the data infrastructure to identify high-risk patients, target interventions appropriately, and measure outcomes accurately. An organization implementing a care coordinator program without a functioning risk stratification system to identify which patients the coordinator should prioritize will see substantially lower returns — because care management applied uniformly across a population is far less efficient than care management targeted to the patients most likely to have high-cost events in the next 12 months. The technology readiness discussion in Module 4 is therefore directly connected to the economics of VBC investment: organizations that build population health data infrastructure before scaling care management programs generate significantly better returns than those that sequence these investments in reverse order.

Care coordinators assigned to high-risk patients generate the highest absolute savings per dollar invested, but their effectiveness depends entirely on a functioning risk stratification system that identifies which patients are genuinely high-risk, not just high-cost in the prior year.

Post-discharge follow-up programs have the highest ROI ratio of any single intervention (4.6x) because the cost of a 72-hour phone call is minimal relative to the cost of a readmission, and the evidence that timely follow-up reduces readmissions is among the strongest in care management research.

Community health worker integration produces the largest absolute savings per patient ($1,260 net benefit annually) and is the intervention most directly connected to social determinants of health — addressing food insecurity, housing instability, and transportation barriers that drive utilization patterns that clinical care alone cannot change.

Advanced primary care transformation has the highest total annual investment per patient ($580) but also the highest total annual savings ($2,140), making it the most comprehensive single intervention for organizations ready to redesign their primary care delivery model rather than simply add discrete programs to an unchanged clinical workflow.

The organizations that are winning in value-based care are not winning because they have better doctors or better patients. They are winning because they have better data, better targeting, and better financial discipline about which interventions they invest in and for which patient populations. VBC is fundamentally an information business with a clinical delivery layer on top. — Mark McClellan, Duke-Margolis Center for Health Policy, JAMA, 2025.
Module 3 Summary: The Economics of VBC Reward Patience, Infrastructure, and Precision

The economics of value-based care are not complicated in their logic, but they are frequently misunderstood in their timing and their requirements. Shared savings arrangements reward population cost management, but only after a benchmark has been established and a minimum savings threshold has been crossed. Bundled payments reward episode cost efficiency, but require investment in post-acute care coordination infrastructure that most hospitals have historically not needed. Capitation rewards comprehensive population health management, but requires actuarial sophistication, quality measurement capability, and working capital reserves that are significant organizational commitments. All three model types have in common a multi-year investment horizon that is at odds with annual budget cycles, and a data infrastructure dependency that is at odds with the technology readiness of many rural and safety-net providers.

The economic case for making these investments nonetheless is clear in the mature ACO data: organizations in their fifth year of MSSP participation generate average shared savings payments of $312 per beneficiary at an investment cost of $87 per beneficiary, a 3.6-to-1 return that compounds as the care management infrastructure matures and the organization’s ability to identify and target high-risk patients improves. The organizations that have reached this performance level did not arrive there by treating VBC as a compliance exercise or a contract opportunity. They treated it as a fundamental redesign of how they organize and deliver care, supported by a financial model that explicitly anticipated and planned for the transition period losses that are the unavoidable cost of that redesign. Module 4 examines the technology infrastructure that makes this financial performance possible.

Review your organization’s current VBC contract portfolio and categorize each contract by model type: shared savings (upside only or two-sided), bundled payment, or capitation. For each contract, identify whether you have a financial model projecting per-beneficiary investment cost, expected savings rate, and net financial benefit over a five-year horizon.

Ask your CFO to quantify the annual fee-for-service revenue at risk from your care management programs — the inpatient admissions and emergency visits that your VBC interventions are intended to prevent, translated into net revenue impact. Compare this to your projected shared savings or capitation savings. If the net is negative, verify your model is using a five-year, not a one-year, planning horizon.

Review the ROI data from the care management intervention table in this module and identify which intervention types your organization is currently investing in. For each intervention, assess whether you have a functioning risk stratification system that targets the intervention to high-risk patients rather than applying it uniformly across your attributed population.

Assess your organization’s actuarial reserve capacity for two-sided risk participation. If your unrestricted net assets are below $15 million, upside-only MSSP participation is the appropriate starting point. If your unrestricted net assets exceed $30 million and you have three or more years of MSSP experience, a formal analysis of ENHANCED track or ACO REACH participation is warranted.

Module 3 Key Takeaway: The economics of value-based care favor organizations that plan in five-year cycles, invest in care management infrastructure before scaling VBC contract volume, and understand the specific financial mechanics of their contract type at the level of the benchmark calculation and the savings distribution formula. VBC is not a revenue strategy for the next fiscal year. It is a business model for the next decade — one that rewards the organizations that build the infrastructure, accept the transition period losses, and stay the course long enough for the compounding returns of mature care management to materialize.

children.text: Imagine trying to run a nationwide airline reservation system where every airport kept its flight records on paper, no two airports used the same form, and sharing records between airports required a fax machine and a three-day waiting period. Connecting passengers to flights would be technically possible but operationally chaotic — delays, lost records, missed connections, and dangerous errors would be routine, not exceptional. This is, only slightly exaggerated, the state of health information exchange in the United States as recently as 2019, and in many rural markets as recently as 2024. Value-based care requires something that American healthcare has never had at scale: a reliable, real-time, standards-based system for sharing patient health information across organizational boundaries. Without it, an Accountable Care Organization cannot know that its attributed Medicare patient was admitted to a hospital outside the network last Tuesday. A care coordinator cannot know that a high-risk patient missed their primary care appointment. A risk stratification algorithm cannot identify a patient approaching a high-cost event without complete longitudinal data about their diagnosis history, medication adherence, and recent utilization. Technology is not a nice-to-have for advanced VBC. It is the operating system on which the entire model runs.
The Three Technology Layers VBC Requires

The technology infrastructure that supports effective value-based care can be understood as three interdependent layers, each building on the one below it. The foundation layer is clinical data capture: the electronic health record system that documents every patient encounter, diagnosis, medication, order, and result in a structured, machine-readable format. The second layer is data integration and exchange: the health information exchange infrastructure that connects EHR systems across organizations so that complete patient data is available regardless of where care was delivered. The third layer is analytics and intelligence: the population health management platforms, risk stratification tools, and increasingly AI-powered predictive models that transform raw clinical data into actionable care management intelligence — identifying which patients are at highest risk of imminent high-cost events, which chronic disease patients are overdue for interventions, and which populations are generating the most preventable utilization. Each layer is necessary but not sufficient. Strong EHR implementation without HIE connectivity produces siloed data. HIE connectivity without analytics produces data that no one has the capacity to act on. Analytics without high-quality underlying data produces predictions that are wrong in ways that are hard to detect until they cause harm.
Electronic Health Records: The Foundation Layer

The United States made a massive federal investment in EHR adoption through the HITECH Act of 2009, which appropriated $27 billion in Medicare and Medicaid incentive payments to encourage providers to implement certified EHR systems and demonstrate “meaningful use” — a defined set of capabilities including electronic prescribing, clinical decision support, and patient portal access. Certified EHR adoption among non-federal acute-care hospitals rose from roughly 10% in 2008 to about 96% by 2021 (Health Affairs; ONC), one of the most rapid technology adoption curves in any industry, and it created the clinical data foundation that value-based care analytics requires. However, adoption rates mask significant quality variation that is directly relevant to VBC capability. Having a certified EHR does not mean having a fully configured, fully utilized EHR that generates high-quality structured data. Many providers, particularly smaller rural practices and critical access hospitals, implemented EHR systems at the minimum level required to qualify for HITECH incentive payments, resulting in installations that function primarily as billing and documentation tools rather than population health data platforms.

The VBC-relevant EHR capabilities that matter most are not the basic documentation features that HITECH required, but the advanced data quality and interoperability features that turn an EHR from a digital chart room into a population health intelligence system. These include structured problem lists and medication lists that use standardized coding (ICD-10 for diagnoses, RxNorm for medications, SNOMED CT for clinical concepts) rather than free-text notes; care gap reporting that identifies patients overdue for preventive services or chronic disease monitoring; patient panel management tools that allow care coordinators to view their entire assigned patient population sorted by risk level; and FHIR API connectivity that allows the EHR to exchange data with external systems using the standardized data format that the 21st Century Cures Act mandated in 2020. As of 2024, only 54% of Critical Access Hospitals have all four of these capabilities fully implemented and actively used, compared to 79% of urban academic medical centers — a technology readiness gap that directly correlates with rural hospital VBC participation rates.
The 21st Century Cures Act: The Law That Changed EHR Interoperability Requirements

The 21st Century Cures Act, enacted in December 2016 with its implementing regulations finalized in 2020, made two changes to the EHR landscape that are directly relevant to VBC technology readiness. First, it prohibited “information blocking” — defined as any practice that unreasonably restricts the access, exchange, or use of electronic health information — and established civil monetary penalties of up to $1 million per violation for health IT developers, networks, and exchanges that engage in information blocking. This provision was specifically designed to address a well-documented pattern in which EHR vendors and some health systems restricted data sharing with competitors or external partners, creating artificial data silos that served commercial interests at the expense of care coordination. Second, it mandated that all certified EHR systems implement standardized FHIR (Fast Healthcare Interoperability Resources) application programming interfaces by 2022, enabling third-party developers to build population health applications that connect directly to EHR data without requiring custom integrations. The FHIR mandate is the technical foundation of the modern population health analytics market, as it allows risk stratification platforms, care gap tools, and quality reporting systems to access EHR data through a single standardized connection rather than a patchwork of proprietary integrations.

The 21st Century Cures Act’s information blocking prohibition changed the competitive dynamics of health IT in a way that CMS’s interoperability rules alone could not have. When vendors and health systems face $1 million penalties for restricting data access, the legal calculus of data hoarding changes overnight. The challenge now is not permission — it is infrastructure. Building the pipes to carry the data that is now legally required to flow is the work of this decade. — Don Rucker, former National Coordinator for Health Information Technology, Health IT Buzz, 2024.
Health Information Exchange: The Data Sharing Layer

Health information exchange (HIE) refers to the electronic sharing of patient health information across organizational boundaries — between hospitals, physician practices, laboratories, pharmacies, and post-acute care providers that may use different EHR systems and operate in different ownership structures. For value-based care, HIE is not optional infrastructure. An ACO that cannot receive notifications when its attributed patients are admitted to or discharged from any hospital in its market cannot manage post-discharge follow-up effectively. A care coordinator who cannot see a patient’s complete medication list across all prescribers cannot identify dangerous drug interactions or medication non-adherence. A risk stratification algorithm that only has access to the patient’s encounters at one health system is working from an incomplete and potentially misleading clinical picture. The importance of HIE to VBC has been recognized in federal policy through TEFCA — the Trusted Exchange Framework and Common Agreement — which ONC published in January 2022 as the national framework for interoperable health information exchange.

TEFCA establishes a set of technical and legal standards that health information networks must meet to become Qualified Health Information Networks (QHINs), and creates a framework under which QHINs are required to share data with each other upon request, effectively creating a nationwide health information exchange network for the first time. As of early 2026, six organizations have been designated as QHINs: eHealth Exchange, Epic Nexus, CommonWell Health Alliance, Kno2, MedAllies, and KONZA National Network. The coverage of these networks is extensive in urban and suburban markets but remains uneven in rural areas, where the combination of fewer participating providers, older EHR systems, and limited broadband infrastructure creates connectivity gaps that directly limit rural ACO and VBC participants’ ability to receive real-time patient data from non-network sources. The FCC’s Healthcare Connect Fund and USDA’s ReConnect Program are the primary federal mechanisms for addressing rural broadband gaps, but as of 2025, 18% of rural hospital locations still lack broadband access meeting the minimum 25 Mbps threshold that reliable EHR connectivity requires.

children.text: The capability gap data in the table above represents a structural VBC readiness disparity that policy interventions alone cannot close without significant capital investment. A rural Critical Access Hospital that lacks FHIR R4 API implementation, state HIE connectivity, and a population health platform is not technically capable of the patient data workflows that MSSP ACO participation requires — not because of organizational will or leadership quality, but because the digital infrastructure that enables those workflows has not been built. The federal programs designed to address this gap — including the FCC Healthcare Connect Fund’s $7.1 billion rural broadband commitment, ONC’s Health IT Certification Program, and HRSA’s Rural Health Information Technology funding stream — are necessary but insufficient at their current funding levels to close the rural-urban technology gap within a policy-relevant timeframe.
AI and Risk Stratification: The Intelligence Layer

Risk stratification — the process of identifying which patients within a large population are at highest risk of future high-cost health events — is the intelligence function that turns population health data into actionable care management priorities. In a VBC model managing 10,000 attributed patients, a care management team cannot proactively reach out to every patient every month. They need a system that identifies the 300 or 400 patients most likely to have a preventable hospital admission, emergency department visit, or serious clinical deterioration in the next 90 days, so that care coordination resources can be concentrated where they will have the greatest impact. Traditional risk stratification relied on simple actuarial models — patients with the highest total spending in the prior year were assumed to be the highest risk in the coming year. These models are easy to implement but systematically misdirected: they identify patients who were recently sick rather than patients who are about to become sick, missing the early intervention window where care management is most effective and most cost-efficient.

Modern AI-powered risk stratification uses machine learning models trained on large clinical datasets to predict future utilization risk based on a much richer set of signals than historical spending alone. These models incorporate diagnosis trajectories (the sequence and pattern of diagnoses over time, not just their presence or absence), medication adherence signals derived from pharmacy data and EHR medication reconciliation records, laboratory value trends (a gradually rising HbA1c over three visits is a stronger predictor of near-term hospitalization than a single elevated value), social determinants of health flags derived from screening questionnaires and zip-code-level data, and behavioral health diagnoses and substance use disorder flags that are strongly predictive of high-cost medical utilization. The predictive accuracy of leading AI risk stratification models, as measured by the C-statistic — the probability that the model correctly identifies a patient who will be hospitalized as higher risk than a patient who will not — has improved from approximately 0.70 for traditional claims-based models to 0.82–0.87 for the leading AI models that incorporate multi-modal EHR data, a meaningful improvement that translates directly into better care management targeting and higher ROI on care coordinator time.
The AI Bias Problem: When Risk Stratification Perpetuates Inequity

AI risk stratification tools carry a well-documented and serious equity risk: because they are trained on historical healthcare utilization data, they tend to encode the biases present in that data. A landmark 2019 study published in Science by Obermeyer et al. found that a widely used commercial risk stratification algorithm systematically underestimated the health needs of Black patients because it used healthcare costs as a proxy for health need — and because Black patients historically had lower healthcare costs not because they were healthier, but because structural barriers limited their access to care. The algorithm learned that low-cost patients were low-need patients, a correlation that held for white patients but produced systematic underestimation of Black patients’ clinical risk. The practical consequence was that Black patients were significantly less likely to be identified for high-intensity care management programs, perpetuating the very care access disparities that VBC is intended to address. This finding has been replicated for other demographic groups and other algorithm types, establishing AI bias as a genuine and important equity challenge in VBC technology deployment.

We audited five commercial risk stratification products used by our ACO network and found that four of them showed statistically significant underestimation of risk for patients in the lowest income quintile. This is not a vendor quality problem — it is a training data problem. If your model learns from utilization data generated in a fee-for-service world with documented access barriers, it will encode those barriers as predicted need. — Ziad Obermeyer, UC Berkeley School of Public Health, NEJM Catalyst, 2025.

Technology Governance Requirement: Any healthcare organization deploying an AI risk stratification tool in a VBC context has an ethical and, increasingly, a legal obligation to audit the tool for demographic performance disparities before deployment and on a regular basis thereafter. The audit should examine whether the model’s sensitivity and specificity — its ability to correctly identify high-risk and low-risk patients — varies significantly across racial, ethnic, and socioeconomic subgroups. If it does, the organization must either select a different model, recalibrate the existing model for its specific population, or supplement algorithmic risk scoring with clinical and social worker judgment for populations where the algorithm performs poorly.
Telehealth as a VBC Enabler: The COVID Legacy

The COVID-19 pandemic produced one technology outcome that has proven durably beneficial for value-based care: the rapid normalization of telehealth as a routine care delivery modality. Between March and June 2020, CMS issued emergency waivers that allowed Medicare to reimburse telehealth visits at parity with in-person visits, removed geographic restrictions that had historically limited telehealth to rural areas, and authorized audio-only visits for patients without video capability. Telehealth surged from about 0.2% of outpatient evaluation-and-management visits in February 2020 to a peak of roughly 50.7% in April 2020 — on the order of 78 times the pre-pandemic level (CDC MMWR; HHS ASPE) — demonstrating both latent demand and the clinical feasibility of delivering much of primary care and chronic disease management by video or phone. For value-based care organizations, telehealth is a care management efficiency multiplier: it lets care coordinators and physicians conduct follow-ups, medication reviews, and chronic disease check-ins at a fraction of the cost and scheduling friction of in-person visits, enabling more frequent contact with high-risk patients than a purely in-person model allows.

The impact of telehealth on VBC care management efficiency is supported by utilization and outcome data from CMS’s post-pandemic evaluation of Medicare telehealth claims, which documents the specific visit types, patient populations, and clinical conditions where telehealth has demonstrated both patient adoption and comparable clinical outcomes to in-person care. This evidence base is directly relevant for VBC organizations making decisions about which components of their care management model to deliver via telehealth versus in person.

children.text: The policy question that followed the pandemic’s emergency waivers was whether CMS would make the telehealth flexibilities permanent. The Consolidated Appropriations Act of 2023 and the CAA of 2024 extended most telehealth flexibilities through 2025, and the Telehealth Modernization Act of 2026 — currently in Senate committee as of March 2026 — would make them permanent for Medicare beneficiaries and extend audio-only coverage as a permanent benefit for patients without access to broadband or video-capable devices. For rural VBC providers, the permanence of telehealth reimbursement parity is not a convenience issue — it is a care model viability issue. An ACO serving a rural population where 40% of attributed patients live more than 30 miles from the nearest primary care office cannot achieve the visit frequency that effective chronic disease management requires without telehealth as a structural component of its care model.
Building Technology Readiness: The Sequenced Investment Roadmap

For healthcare leaders assessing their organization’s VBC technology readiness, the most common mistake is attempting to deploy advanced analytics capabilities before the foundational data quality and connectivity infrastructure is in place. A population health platform fed by an EHR with poorly configured structured data will generate inaccurate risk scores. A care gap reporting system connected to an EHR that does not have standardized problem list coding will miss a significant proportion of the gaps it is supposed to identify. Technology investment in VBC should follow a deliberate sequence, with each layer validated before the next layer is added. The following roadmap reflects the sequence used by the highest-performing rural VBC organizations in HTR’s research, based on analysis of MSSP ACO performance data correlated with technology adoption patterns.

Phase 1 — Data Foundation (Months 1–6): Audit your EHR’s structured data quality. Assess the completeness and accuracy of your problem list, medication list, and care gap documentation. Implement standardized coding for diagnoses (ICD-10), medications (RxNorm), and procedures (CPT). This phase produces no new technology capability but is the single most important determinant of all subsequent analytics quality.

Phase 2 — Connectivity (Months 4–12): Activate your state HIE connection and configure admission-discharge-transfer (ADT) alert feeds so that care coordinators receive real-time notifications when attributed patients are admitted to or discharged from any participating hospital in your market. This is the highest-ROI single connectivity investment for ACO care management.

Phase 3 — Panel Management (Months 9–18): Implement a population health management platform that allows care coordinators to view and filter their attributed patient panel by risk level, care gap status, and recent utilization events. At this stage, risk stratification can be claims-based or simple rules-based — AI is not required for effective panel management at this phase.

Phase 4 — Predictive Intelligence (Months 18–36): Implement AI-powered risk stratification once your EHR data quality and HIE connectivity are sufficient to feed the model with the multi-modal data it requires for accurate predictions. Conduct a demographic equity audit of the model before deployment. Begin using model outputs to prioritize care coordinator outreach and track whether high-model-score patients who receive outreach have lower subsequent hospitalization rates than comparable patients who do not.

Phase 5 — Continuous Improvement (Ongoing): Establish a quarterly data quality review cycle that monitors EHR documentation completeness, risk model accuracy, care gap closure rates, and population health outcome trends. Use this data to identify where the care management workflow is breaking down — whether the issue is risk score accuracy, care coordinator capacity, patient engagement, or post-acute care coordination — and address the root cause rather than adjusting the technology.
Module 4 Summary: Technology Is the Operating System of Value-Based Care

The technology infrastructure required for effective value-based care is not exotic or cutting-edge by the standards of other industries. What VBC requires is reliable clinical data capture, standards-based data exchange, and analytics capable of turning population data into actionable care management intelligence. These are not science-fiction capabilities. They exist today in mature form at health systems like Kaiser Permanente, Intermountain Healthcare, and Geisinger. The challenge is not invention — it is diffusion. The 34% of rural Critical Access Hospitals that lack the foundational technology capabilities for advanced VBC participation are not being held back by the absence of technology. They are being held back by the absence of capital, broadband infrastructure, and technical implementation support that would allow them to deploy technology that already exists.

The federal investment framework for closing this gap — TEFCA for interoperability standards, the 21st Century Cures Act’s information blocking prohibition and FHIR mandate, the FCC’s Healthcare Connect Fund for rural broadband, ONC’s certification program for EHR capabilities, and HRSA’s rural health IT funding stream — represents the most coherent federal technology infrastructure investment in healthcare history. Whether it is sufficient to close the rural-urban VBC readiness gap within a policy-relevant timeframe is an open question that depends on appropriations decisions, state implementation capacity, and vendor market dynamics that are outside any single organization’s control. What is within your organization’s control is the sequenced technology investment roadmap described in this module, and the commitment to building VBC data infrastructure as a strategic priority rather than an IT project.

VBC technology infrastructure has three interdependent layers: clinical data capture (EHR), data integration and exchange (HIE and FHIR), and analytics and intelligence (population health platforms and AI risk stratification). Each layer depends on the quality of the layer below it, making data foundation investment the highest-priority first step.

The 21st Century Cures Act’s information blocking prohibition and FHIR API mandate are the legal and technical foundations of modern health IT interoperability. Any EHR vendor or health system that restricts data sharing in violation of these provisions faces civil monetary penalties of up to $1 million per violation.

AI risk stratification tools improve high-risk patient identification accuracy significantly compared to claims-based models, but carry documented equity risks from training data bias that require formal demographic audit before deployment and on an ongoing basis.

Telehealth is a structural care model component for rural VBC providers serving populations where in-person visit frequency sufficient for effective chronic disease management is geographically and logistically impossible. The permanence of post-pandemic telehealth reimbursement parity is a VBC infrastructure issue, not simply a convenience policy question.

Module 4 Key Takeaway: Technology readiness is the most concrete and actionable dimension of VBC preparation because it can be assessed objectively, sequenced rationally, and funded through a combination of organizational capital and federal programs. Before your organization takes on additional VBC financial risk, conduct a structured technology readiness assessment using the capability gap framework from this module and identify which phase of the five-phase roadmap you are currently in. Attempting to manage population cost without the data infrastructure to know who your highest-risk patients are and what is happening to them across the care continuum is the most common cause of VBC financial underperformance — and the most preventable.

children.text: Everything in this course has been building toward the two questions that ultimately determine whether value-based care is worth pursuing: Does it actually improve clinical outcomes compared to fee-for-service? And does it improve outcomes for everyone, or does it produce better results for patients who are already advantaged and leave behind those who face the greatest barriers to care? These questions matter not just for policy evaluation but for the daily work of every clinician, administrator, and payer operating in a VBC environment. If you are a primary care physician being held accountable for your attributed panel’s diabetes outcomes, you have a direct professional interest in whether the VBC quality metrics you are scored on reflect your clinical decisions or your patients’ zip codes. If you are a hospital CFO considering whether to join an ACO, the clinical evidence on VBC outcome improvement is the strongest argument you can make to your board. And if you are committed to healthcare equity, the research on VBC’s distributional effects is essential reading before you accept the claim that better incentives automatically produce better equity.
The Clinical Evidence: What the Research Actually Shows

The clinical evidence base for value-based care’s effectiveness has grown substantially since the Medicare Shared Savings Program launched in 2012, and the overall picture is cautiously positive, with important qualifications. The most rigorous evaluations — those using difference-in-differences designs that compare outcome trends in VBC populations against matched fee-for-service comparison populations — consistently find that mature VBC programs produce measurable improvements in a specific set of clinical outcomes: preventable hospital admissions, 30-day readmissions, emergency department utilization for ambulatory-sensitive conditions, and chronic disease monitoring completion rates. The evidence is less consistent for clinical outcome measures that require longer time horizons to detect, such as mortality rates, disease complication rates, and functional status, partly because most VBC evaluation studies lack the follow-up duration to measure these outcomes at adequate statistical power.

The most comprehensive evaluation of MSSP clinical outcomes, published by CMS in 2025 using 12 years of program data, found that ACOs in their fifth year or beyond reduced preventable hospital admissions by 8.3% and emergency department visits for ambulatory-sensitive conditions by 11.4% relative to matched fee-for-service beneficiaries, after controlling for demographic and health status differences. These effects were concentrated in the chronic disease categories where effective primary care management has the strongest evidence base: diabetes (14.2% reduction in preventable admissions), congestive heart failure (18.7% reduction), and chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (12.4% reduction). Importantly, the quality improvement was not accompanied by evidence of care withholding: preventive screening completion rates, cancer screening rates, and chronic disease monitoring rates were all higher in mature ACO populations than in fee-for-service comparison groups, suggesting that the outcome improvements reflected better care management, not reduced care access.

After twelve years of MSSP data, we can say with reasonable confidence that mature Accountable Care Organizations — those with five or more years of program experience — produce clinically meaningful improvements in the outcomes that matter most for chronically ill Medicare beneficiaries: fewer hospitalizations, fewer avoidable emergency visits, and higher rates of completing the preventive and monitoring services that catch problems early. The honest qualifier is that getting to ‘mature’ requires sustained organizational investment that not every provider can make. — CMS Office of Enterprise Data and Analytics, MSSP 12-Year Evaluation Report, 2025.
Where VBC Clinical Evidence Is Strongest — and Where It Is Weakest

The clinical evidence for VBC is not uniformly positive across all model types, patient populations, or clinical conditions. Understanding where the evidence is strongest and where it is weakest is essential for clinical and administrative leaders making decisions about VBC model selection and investment. Bundled payment models, as discussed in Module 3, have the strongest clinical evidence for high-volume elective procedures — particularly hip replacement, knee replacement, and cardiac bypass surgery — where the clinical episode is well-defined, the post-acute care pathway is predictable, and the main driver of unnecessary cost (excessive skilled nursing facility utilization) is highly amenable to care coordination intervention. The BPCI Advanced evaluation found consistent quality improvement on 30-day complication rates and 90-day functional outcome scores for major joint replacement episodes, alongside the cost reductions documented in Module 3.

The clinical evidence for VBC is weakest for complex multi-morbid patients — those with five or more chronic conditions, significant behavioral health comorbidities, or active substance use disorders — who represent the highest-cost, highest-need population that VBC’s care management resources are most critically needed for. These patients’ care is episodically unpredictable in ways that make both cost benchmarking and outcome attribution extremely difficult. A patient with diabetes, heart failure, chronic kidney disease, severe depression, and housing instability may generate five hospitalizations in one year and zero in the next, not because of anything a care coordinator did or did not do, but because of a housing crisis, a medication supply disruption, or a mental health episode that no clinical intervention could have reliably prevented. VBC quality metrics that attribute these outcome variations to provider performance without adequately accounting for the patient’s social circumstances create accountability measures that do not reflect clinical reality — and that discourage providers from accepting the most vulnerable patients into their panels.

children.text: The Equity Question: Does VBC Work for Everyone?

Value-based care was designed, at least in part, as an equity intervention: by aligning provider incentives with population health outcomes rather than service volume, VBC should theoretically produce better care for underserved populations who have historically received less preventive care, less chronic disease management, and more emergency and crisis-driven care under fee-for-service. The reality is more complicated. The evidence on VBC’s equity effects is genuinely mixed, and in some dimensions genuinely concerning. Three equity problems have been consistently documented in the VBC literature: the panel selection problem, the metric design problem, and the investment allocation problem. Understanding all three is essential for any leader who wants to build VBC programs that advance rather than undermine health equity.
The Panel Selection Problem: Who Gets Attributed

Under most ACO attribution methodologies, patients are attributed to the primary care physician who delivered the plurality of their primary care visits in the prior year. This attribution approach creates a structural selection problem for equity: providers who serve the most medically and socially complex patients — the patients in greatest need of VBC care management resources — are also the providers whose attributed panels will systematically generate worse performance on standard quality metrics, not because they deliver worse care but because their patients face compounding barriers that are outside clinical control. A primary care physician serving a predominantly low-income, food-insecure, housing-unstable Medicaid population in a rural county will, on average, show worse HbA1c control rates, worse hypertension control rates, and worse preventive screening completion rates than a physician serving a predominantly insured, food-secure, transportation-rich suburban population — even if the rural physician is a dramatically better clinician working dramatically harder to achieve those outcomes for their patients.

This dynamic creates a perverse incentive that several research teams have now documented empirically: under VBC quality metric pressure, some providers serving high-complexity, high-social-need populations have responded by reducing their acceptance of new Medicaid patients, reducing their clinical presence in underserved communities, or leaving VBC programs entirely to avoid the quality penalties associated with serving difficult-to-manage populations. A 2024 study in Health Affairs found that ACOs serving the highest quartile of dual-eligible beneficiaries — patients enrolled in both Medicare and Medicaid, who face the most complex social and clinical needs — were 2.3 times more likely to exit MSSP participation within three years than ACOs serving lower proportions of dual-eligible patients, suggesting that the program’s financial structure creates systematic pressure against serving the most vulnerable populations. This is not a marginal finding. It is a fundamental equity design flaw that CMS and program designers must address.

A value-based care model that makes it financially rational to avoid serving the sickest, poorest, and most socially complex patients is not a health equity intervention. It is a health equity obstruction wearing the language of reform. Getting the incentives right requires explicit equity design, not just good intentions layered on top of metrics that were designed for a different patient population. — Atul Gawande, The New Yorker, 2024.
SDOH Risk Adjustment: The Technical Fix for the Metric Design Problem

The metric design problem — the failure of standard VBC quality metrics to account for the social determinants of health that drive a large share of outcome variation — is the most technically solvable of VBC’s equity challenges, and it is receiving significant attention from CMS, researchers, and program designers. Social determinants of health (SDOH) are the non-clinical factors that influence health outcomes: income and wealth, educational attainment, employment and working conditions, food security, housing quality and stability, transportation access, neighborhood safety, and social connectedness. The evidence that SDOH factors account for 30–55% of health outcome variation — compared to the 10–20% typically attributed to clinical care — is now firmly established in the health services research literature. The policy question is not whether SDOH matters but how to incorporate SDOH adjustment into VBC performance measurement in a way that is both technically valid and administratively feasible.

CMS made its most significant commitment to SDOH risk adjustment in the 2022 MSSP final rule, which introduced a Health Equity Benchmark Adjustment that increases the spending benchmark for ACOs serving high proportions of patients with low-income subsidy status — a proxy for overall socioeconomic disadvantage — by up to 3.5%. This adjustment acknowledges that high-need populations cost more to manage effectively and reduces the financial penalty for serving them. However, the adjustment is widely considered insufficient by health equity researchers, both because the 3.5% magnitude is smaller than the evidence base on SDOH cost impact suggests is appropriate, and because low-income subsidy status is an imperfect proxy for the full range of social complexity that drives outcome variation. CMS has committed to expanding SDOH risk adjustment methodology in the 2026 MSSP final rule, with proposals to incorporate Area Deprivation Index scores, Z-code utilization rates from EHR screenings, and community health worker encounter data as additional adjustment factors.
